hot_topics.topic: Agentic automation UX and human oversight of AI agents
hot_topics.why_now: Tool-calling LLM agents crossed from demo to deployed product in 2025, so the open problem stopped being 'can the agent act' and became 'how does a person delegate, interrupt, inspect and take back control'. Interaction design, not model capability, is now the bottleneck.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: CHI 2026 (Barcelona, 13-17 April 2026) accepted-workshop list carries a cluster of these: W2 'Agentic Automation Experiences: Rethinking the Interaction of Humans and AI Agents', W30 'From Human-Human Collaboration to Human-Agent Collaboration', W39 'Human-Centered Explainable AI (HCXAI): Re-examining XAI in the Era of Agentic AI', and W4 'AI CHAOS! 2nd Workshop on the Challenges for Human Oversight of AI Systems'. UIST 2025 main track includes 'agentAR: Creating Augmented Reality Applications with Tool-Augmented LLM-based Autonomous Agents'.
hot_topics.one_line: The research question has shifted from making AI agents capable to designing the controls, interruptions and explanations a human needs to safely hand work to one.

hot_topics.topic: Human-centered evaluation, auditing and red-teaming of language models
hot_topics.why_now: Automated benchmarks visibly failed to predict deployed behavior, so HCI is claiming evaluation as its own object of study: who the human experts are, how audits get staffed, and how red-teaming scales when the system under test is itself an agent.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: CHI 2026 W59 'Third Workshop on Human-Centered Evaluation and Auditing of Language Models: AI Agents-in-the-Loop' (third edition, so the community is established) alongside first-edition CHI 2026 W36 'Human Expertise for AI Red-Teaming and Scalable Evaluation'. Recent arXiv cs.HC submissions retrieved 2026-07-27 include 'HARP: The Human-AI Research Platform' and 'AI Assistants Overassist', a benchmark comparing LLM tutor intervention rates against human teachers.
hot_topics.one_line: Evaluating an AI system is being treated as a human process to be designed and studied, not a script to be run.

hot_topics.topic: LLMs as simulated research participants (synthetic personas as method)
hot_topics.why_now: Cheap persona-conditioned generation made it tempting to replace survey and interview participants with model output, and 2025-2026 produced both the tooling and the first serious psychometric rebuttals, so the field is now fighting over whether the method is admissible at all.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Two first-edition CHI 2026 workshops attack this directly: W68 'Workshop on Developing Standards and Documentation For LLM Use as Simulated Research Participants' and W29 'From Generation to Simulation: Responsible Use of AI Personas in Human-Centered Design and Research'. Recent arXiv cs.HC submissions retrieved 2026-07-27 show both sides: 'Anamnesis: An Open-Source Platform for Large-Scale Backstory-Conditioned Survey Simulation' and 'PERSONAJUDGE: Simulating Individual Human Preference Judgments' versus 'Personality Without Persons? A Psychometric Critique of Big Five Testing in Large Language Models'.
hot_topics.one_line: Researchers are testing whether a language model prompted to act like a person can stand in for a real study participant, and whether that is science or wishful thinking.
hot_topics.critic_note: Venue evidence is the most precisely accurate in the whole set, and the maturity claim is still wrong. Confirmed verbatim on chi2026.acm.org/workshops/accepted (69 workshops): W68 'Workshop on Developing Standards and Documentation For LLM Use as Simulated Research Participants' and W29 'From Generation to Simulation: Responsible Use of AI Personas in Human-Centered Design and Research'. Disqualifying: a survey exists, 'From Individual to Society: A Survey on Social Simulation Driven by Large Language Model-based Agents' (2412.03563, Dec 2024), plus a review at 2310.17888 (Oct 2023). The specific claim that 2025-2026 'produced the first serious psychometric rebuttals' is false: 2302.07267 (Feb 2023, diminished diversity-of-thought) and 2405.07248 (May 2024, 'Limited Ability of LLMs to Simulate Human Psychological Behaviours: a Psychometric Analysis') both predate that window. The fight is three years old, not new.

hot_topics.topic: Agentic visualization: LLM agents that author and reason over charts
hot_topics.why_now: Multimodal models got good enough to read a chart and write chart specifications, so the visualization community moved from 'natural language to chart' toward autonomous agents that take a dataset plus a question and return a whole visual report, plus the benchmarks needed to check whether the agent actually read the data.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: VISxGenAI, the '2nd Workshop on GenAI, Agents, and the Future of VIS', runs 9 November 2026 co-located with IEEE VIS 2026 (Boston) and adds a new 'AgenticVIS Challenge' where 'Participants will develop agents that take datasets and guiding questions as input and generate visual data reports as output' (submissions due 15 August 2026). VISxGenAI also appeared in the IEEE VIS 2025 workshop slate. Supporting arXiv cs.HC work retrieved 2026-07-27: 'VisCanvas: A Node-based Interface for Exploratory Visualization Authoring with LLMs', 'Visualization Autocomplete', 'Flint: A Semantics-Driven Data Visualization Intermediate Language', 'Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy'.
hot_topics.one_line: AI agents are being built to do the whole analysis-to-chart pipeline themselves, which forces the question of how you check that the chart is honest.
hot_topics.critic_note: Self-refuting on its own evidence. Confirmed on ieeevis.org/year/2026/info/program/workshops: the entry reads 'VISxGenAI: 2nd GenAI, Agents, and the Future of VIS'. A second-edition workshop is not a forming signal, and the claim concedes it ran at VIS 2025. Disqualifying independently: 'AI4VIS: Survey on Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Data Visualization' (2102.01330) was submitted Feb 2021 and accepted to IEEE TVCG, so the survey is five and a half years old. VIS 2026 also lists VISxAI at its NINTH edition, EduVis 4th, AccessViz 3rd, which is the profile of a settled sub-community. Genuinely new: only the AgenticVIS Challenge. Unchecked: the Nov 9 2026 date, the Boston venue, and the Aug 15 2026 submission deadline did not appear on the workshop list page I fetched.

hot_topics.topic: Generative UI: interfaces synthesized at runtime rather than designed in advance
hot_topics.why_now: Models can now emit working interface code fast enough to generate a UI per user, per task, per moment, which breaks the profession's core assumption that someone designs a fixed screen ahead of time. The community is still at the stage of asking what the term even means for practice.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: CHI 2026 W66 is literally framed as an open question: 'What does Generative UI mean for HCI Practice?', a first-edition workshop; the adjacent CHI 2026 W38 'Human-AI-UI Interactions Across Modalities' covers the multimodal side. CHI 2026 also restructured into 'a newly refactored program' of six submission areas (Papers, Posters, Interactive Demos, Panels, Workshops, Meetups), widening room for this kind of practice-facing topic.
hot_topics.one_line: Instead of a designer building one screen for everyone, the software generates a different interface on the fly for each person and situation.

hot_topics.topic: Agentic and multimodal AI as assistive technology, including its failure modes
hot_topics.why_now: Vision-language models put scene description and agentic tool use on a phone or headset, which for the first time lets blind and low-vision users build their own assistive tools instead of waiting for one to ship. The same models hallucinate, so trust calibration became an accessibility research problem rather than an ML one.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: UIST 2025 (210 accepted papers, 22.2% acceptance) main track includes 'This is My Fault, Really? Understanding Blind and Low-Vision People's Perception of Hallucination in Large Vision Language Models', 'Accessibility Scout: Personalized Accessibility Scans of Built Environments', and 'AROMA: Mixed-Initiative AI Assistance for Non-Visual Cooking by Grounding Multimodal Information Between Reality and Videos'. Recent arXiv cs.HC submissions retrieved 2026-07-27 include 'Bespoke Visual Assistance: What and How do Blind and Low-Vision People Create with Agentic Programming?', 'Sonic Stage: Automatically Generating Interactive Spatial Soundscapes to Facilitate Dialogue Video Comprehension for Blind Viewers', and 'Reimagining the Augmented Reality Accessibility Ecosystem for Deaf Students'. ASSETS 2025 was held 26-29 October 2025 in Denver (27th edition); I could not retrieve its session list, so the ASSETS-specific detail here is unverified.
hot_topics.one_line: Disabled users are now building their own AI assistants by talking to a model, and the new research problem is what happens when that assistant confidently describes something that is not there.

hot_topics.topic: Accessible and cross-modal data visualization (sonification, haptics, touch)
hot_topics.why_now: Charts are the least accessible common artifact on the web, and cheap text-to-audio plus better haptic hardware finally made non-visual chart representation buildable at scale rather than bespoke per study.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: AccessViz runs as the '3rd Workshop on Accessible Data Visualization' at IEEE VIS 2026, having also appeared in the IEEE VIS 2025 workshop slate; its stated topics include 'Transformation between different information modalities (visualization, sonification, haptics)' and 'Community-centered accessibility practices and participatory design'. On the modality side, CHI 2026 lists first-edition workshops W17 'Cross-Sensory Futures: Rewiring Perception in HCI' and W5 'AI for Haptics and Haptics for AI: Challenges and Opportunities'.
hot_topics.one_line: Work on letting people who cannot see a chart still get its information, by turning data into sound, touch or speech instead of pixels.

hot_topics.topic: 3D Gaussian splatting as the default capture-and-render substrate
hot_topics.why_now: 3DGS trains in minutes and renders in real time on consumer hardware, so between 2024 and 2026 it displaced NeRF as the working representation. The live problems are now downstream engineering, compression, streaming, editing, physics and relighting, which is exactly what a mainstream technique looks like.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: arXiv cs.GR most-recent submissions retrieved 2026-07-27 are saturated with it: 'TopoGS: Planar Reconstruction via Topology-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting', 'ECoNGS: Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats for Volume Visualization', 'Packet-Loss Robust 3D Gaussian Compression via Atomic Packaging and GNN-based Error Concealment', 'Rendering 3D Gaussians on a Graph Processor', 'Instant NuRec: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Reconstruction for Driving Scene Simulation', 'Bake It Till You Make It: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting', '3D-GIMP: When 3D Gaussian Inpainting Meets PatchMatch'. SIGGRAPH 2026 (Los Angeles, 19-23 July 2026) frames its program around 'AI, robotics, immersive experiences, simulation, animation, and cutting-edge innovations in real time'. I state this as mainstream, not hot-and-new: the survey-and-engineering phase is well underway.
hot_topics.one_line: A scene is stored as millions of fuzzy colored blobs instead of triangles, which turns out to be far faster to capture from photos and to draw in real time.

hot_topics.topic: Gaussian-splat avatars and volumetric telepresence for XR
hot_topics.why_now: Splatting made photoreal full-body avatars cheap enough to drive from headset tracking alone, so the unsolved part moved to the network: streaming a live volumetric person under fluctuating bandwidth, which is a systems and codec problem the XR community had previously deferred.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: A dense 2025-2026 arXiv run surfaced via alphaXiv on 2026-07-27: 'VRGaussianAvatar: Integrating 3D Gaussian Avatars into VR' (ETH Zurich, KAIST, Hansung University, 2026-02-02), 'Mon3tr: Monocular 3D Telepresence with Pre-built Gaussian Avatars as Amortization' (2026-01-12), 'ProgressiveAvatars: Progressive Animatable 3D Gaussian Avatars' (2026-03-17), 'CAGS: Color-Adaptive Volumetric Video Streaming with Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting' (2026-05-10), 'Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting enabled Semantic Coding for Real-Time Immersive Video Communications' (2026-04-28), 'TaoAvatar' (Alibaba Group, 2025-03-21), 'GS-Verse: Mesh-based Gaussian Splatting for Physics-aware Interaction in Virtual Reality' (2025-10-13). Venue-side: IEEE VR 2026 (workshops 21-22 March 2026) runs the 'First IEEE XR Workshop on Networking and Sensing for the Metaverse and Multi-user and Social XR Environments' and 'The 5th International Workshop on Intelligent Immersive Media Communications (IIMC2026)'.
hot_topics.one_line: Photoreal 3D copies of real people are now cheap enough to render live in a headset, so the hard part is squeezing them down a normal internet connection.

hot_topics.topic: Generative AI inside XR authoring and runtime (GenAI-XR)
hot_topics.why_now: Text-to-3D and scene generation reached usable quality at the same moment passthrough headsets shipped broadly, so an XR experience can now be generated around the user's actual room at runtime instead of being modeled by an artist beforehand.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: IEEE VR 2026 (workshops 21-22 March 2026) runs 'GenAI-XR: Generative Artificial Intelligence meets Extended Reality' as a newly listed workshop, alongside 'Hardware-Software-Service Co-Design for Practical Extended Reality Systems' and 'Third International Workshop on Perception-driven Graphics and Displays for VR and AR'. CHI 2026 adds W42 'Next Steps for Augmented Reality On-the-Move: Challenges and Opportunities', W49 'Shaping Future Human Connection: Social Augmentation through XR Technologies', W56 'The Co-Living between Reality and Virtuality as a Daily Routine' and W69 'XR for Challenging Environments'. UIST 2025 supplies main-track instances: 'agentAR' and '3D Sketching + 2D Generative AI for Car Exterior Design'. Recent arXiv cs.GR work retrieved 2026-07-27 includes 'Text2Villa: Hierarchical Generation of 3D Indoor Environments with Physics-Aware Analysis-by-Synthesis' and 'ThinkBLOX: 3D Indoor Scene Generation with Progressive Reasoning'.
hot_topics.one_line: Headset software is starting to generate its 3D worlds on demand from a text prompt and the shape of the room you are standing in.
hot_topics.critic_note: Venue evidence is accurate: I fetched ieeevr.org/2026/program/workshop/ and confirmed 'GenAI-XR: Generative Artificial Intelligence meets Extended Reality' (Sunday 22 March), 'Hardware-Software-Service Co-Design for Practical Extended Reality Systems', and 'Third International Workshop on Perception-driven Graphics and Displays for VR and AR', on 21-22 March as claimed. CHI 2026 W42, W49, W56, W69 also confirmed verbatim. The topic still fails the survey test, badly. arXiv 2511.03282 'When Generative Artificial Intelligence meets Extended Reality: A Systematic Review' (2025-11-05) carries essentially the workshop's own title, eight months before it. Add 2508.03014 'Survey of Large Language Models in Extended Reality' (2025-08-05), 2505.05474 '3D Scene Generation: A Survey' (2025-05-08), 2504.11734 'Recent Advances in 3D Object and Scene Generation: A Survey' (2025-04-16, 218 votes), and 2506.05449 'AI-powered Contextual 3D Environment Generation: A Systematic Review' (2025-06-05). The claim also concedes UIST 2025 main-track instances, which is main-venue presence rather than pre-mainstream. Not checked: the two named UIST 2025 papers.

hot_topics.topic: Environmentally responsible and post-growth design research
hot_topics.subdomain: design research, critical and speculative design
hot_topics.why_now: The compute and water cost of AI became a concrete, publishable number rather than a vague worry, so design research has a fresh target: HCI is asking whether its own AI systems and its own growth-oriented design methods are defensible, and DIS reframed its whole 2026 theme around consequences beyond the interface.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: CHI 2026 lists first-edition W34 'HCI-TERRA: HCI Towards EnviRonmentally Responsible AI' and W18 'Cultivating Pedagogies for Post-Growth HCI', plus W58 'The Quality of Speculation: Common Ground for Speculative Design in Human-Computer Interaction?', W15 'Craft-Based Data Physicalization: Opportunities and Challenges' and W33 'Growing Bio-HCI at CHI'. DIS 2026 (Singapore, 13-17 June 2026) sets its theme as 'Beyond Interaction', examining how interactive systems reach into 'sociocultural, political, economic, and ethical dimensions', and keeps non-traditional formats (Pictorials, Provocations, Zines).
hot_topics.one_line: Designers are asking whether the environmental and social cost of the AI systems they build can be justified, and what design looks like if endless growth is not the goal.
hot_topics.critic_note: Venue evidence verified exactly: chi2026.acm.org/workshops/accepted/ confirms W15 Craft-Based Data Physicalization, W18 Cultivating Pedagogies for Post-Growth HCI, W33 Growing Bio-HCI at CHI, W34 HCI-TERRA, W58 The Quality of Speculation, all verbatim. The maturity call is what fails. This area has a dedicated conference with a full decade behind it: arXiv 2605.30543 'Overview over the first decade of LIMITS' (2026-05-28) reviews ten years of Computing within Limits, whose stated principles are 'questioning endless growth narrative' and scarcity, i.e. the claim's own framing. Sustainable HCI predates even that. The 'compute and water cost became a concrete number' premise is also not 2026: arXiv 2504.00692 'The HCI GenAI CO2ST Calculator' (2025-04-01) and 2501.17980 'Limits to AI Growth' (2025-01-29). Self-disqualifying detail: the claim cites DIS 2026 reframing its entire conference theme around this, which is mainstream adoption, not pre-mainstream. Well over three years hot.

hot_topics.topic: Agentic engineering as a programming-languages problem (types, runtimes and verification for agent systems)
hot_topics.subdomain: AI for code, coding agents and agentic engineering
hot_topics.why_now: Tool-calling agents became cheap and ubiquitous in 2024-2025, so the PL community stopped treating them as an application and started asking for the boring infrastructure: type-safe tool interfaces, memory/state semantics, and static analysis of agent plans. The trigger is that agents now write and run code with real side effects, and prompt-level testing does not scale to that.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: PAgE 2026, 'Principles of Agentic Engineering', INAUGURAL edition co-located with PLDI 2026 (Boulder, 15 June 2026; organizers from Microsoft Research, U. Washington, UC Berkeley). Verified call topics include 'Specifications and type-safe interfaces for tool use', 'Static & dynamic analysis and verification of agentic plans', 'Runtimes, compilers and virtual machines for agentic programs'. Parallel SE-side venues: AGENT 2026 ('Agentic Engineering') and BoatSE 2026 ('Bots and Agents in Software Engineering') at ICSE 2026 (Rio de Janeiro, 12-18 April 2026); AgenticDev and MAS-GAIN workshops at ASE 2026 (Munich, 12-16 Oct 2026). arXiv cs.PL 2026-07-20: 'ETAS: An Effect-Typed Language for Agent Systems'.
hot_topics.one_line: Instead of hoping an AI agent behaves, you give it a programming language whose type system and runtime make illegal tool calls and unsafe plans impossible to express.
hot_topics.critic_note: The narrow PL slice is the defensible part, but the topic as scoped is heavily surveyed. Confirmed on pldi26.sigplan.org: PAgE 2026 (Principles of Agentic Engineering) is listed among PLDI 2026 workshops, Boulder, workshops June 15-16, main conference June 17-19. Confirmed on conf.researchr.org/home/icse-2026: STATIC, AGENT, and BoatSE all present, Rio de Janeiro, April 12-18 2026. Unchecked: I could not confirm the 'INAUGURAL' label, the June 15 date specifically, the organizer affiliations, or the quoted call topics from the index page, and the stated subdomain is 'AI for code, coding agents and agentic engineering', which is squarely surveyed territory: 2408.02479 (Aug 2024), 2409.02977 (Sep 2024, 124 papers), 2409.09030 (Sep 2024), then 2508.00083, 2510.09721, 2512.22256. Two years of survey literature. If the claim were narrowed to effect types and agent runtimes (the ETAS paper), it would be more defensible, but as written it is overstated.

hot_topics.topic: PromptOps and 'vibe coding' as an empirical software-engineering object of study
hot_topics.subdomain: Empirical software engineering and developer studies
hot_topics.why_now: Prompt-first development moved from a meme to a measurable industrial practice during 2025, and the field now has enough repositories and enough burned teams to run controlled experiments on it. The open question shifted from 'can the model write code' to 'what does prompt-driven development do to test discipline, review load and maintenance signals'.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: POVC 2026, 'PromptOps & Vibe Coding' workshop, co-located with ASE 2026 (Munich, 12-16 Oct 2026). arXiv cs.SE 2026-07-22: 'Vibe Coding in Software Development: A Multivocal Literature Review'; arXiv cs.SE 2026-07-24: 'Vibe Coding: An Experiment with Test-Driven Development'; arXiv cs.SE 2026-07-23: 'Maintenance Signals in AI-Assisted GitHub Repositories'; arXiv cs.SE 2026-07-24: '"Go Home Copilot, You're Drunk": Developer Responses to Agent-Generated Comments'. Note the multivocal literature review already exists, which by the survey heuristic means the topic has left 'forming'.
hot_topics.one_line: Researchers are now measuring, with experiments and repository mining, what actually happens to code quality and maintenance when people build software mainly by prompting rather than typing.

hot_topics.topic: Benchmarking and adversarial robustness of coding agents (beyond pass@k)
hot_topics.subdomain: AI for code, coding agents and agentic engineering
hot_topics.why_now: SWE-bench-style leaderboards saturated and got contaminated, so 2026 work moved to multi-domain task suites, harness-effect studies, and deliberately malicious inputs. What got cheap is running an agent end-to-end in a sandboxed repo; what got exposed is that reported scores move with prompt format and harness design as much as with model quality.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: AI-SQE 2026 ('AI for Software Quality Evaluation') and DeepTest 2026 workshops at ICSE 2026; FORGE (AI Foundation Models and Software Engineering) now runs as a co-located conference at ICSE 2026. arXiv cs.SE 2026-07-23: 'Tencent WorkBuddy Bench: Multi-Domain Coding-Agent Benchmark'; 2026-07-22: 'IssueTrojanBench: Benchmarking AI Coding Agents Against Malicious Requests'; 2026-07-23: 'Output Format x Model Identity: Interaction Effects in Coding Agent Performance'; 2026-07-24: 'Claim Plane: Enforceable Change Intents for Parallel Coding Agents'.
hot_topics.one_line: Measuring a coding agent honestly now means testing it on many domains, on hostile inputs, and controlling for the scaffold around it, because the scaffold moves the score as much as the model does.

hot_topics.topic: LLM-generated specifications, proof harnesses and contracts for auto-active verification
hot_topics.why_now: Verification tools like Dafny, Verus and Kani were always bottlenecked on humans writing invariants and harnesses, which is exactly the boring, syntax-heavy work language models do adequately. Because the verifier checks the output, a wrong LLM guess is rejected rather than shipped, so this is one of the few places where unreliable generation is safe by construction.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Dafny 2026 workshop, 'Auto-Active Program Verification', co-located with POPL 2026 (Rennes, France, 11-17 Jan 2026), alongside CPP 2026 and VMCAI 2026 at the same venue. arXiv cs.SE 2026-07-24: 'HarnessLLM: Rust Verification Harness Generation with LLMs'; 2026-07-24: 'KaPilot: LLM-Assisted Generation of Kani Specifications'. arXiv cs.PL 2026-07-19: 'CHC-based Automated Verification of WebAssembly Programs'; 2026-07-16: 'Gradually Verifying Unfolding Expressions & Pure Functions'.
hot_topics.one_line: A language model writes the mathematical annotations a verifier needs, and the verifier throws away anything the model got wrong, so you get machine-checked guarantees without a formal-methods PhD writing every invariant.

hot_topics.topic: Machine-assisted proof engineering and the Rocq/Lean 4 consolidation of mechanized mathematics
hot_topics.subdomain: Proof assistants, type theory and mechanized mathematics
hot_topics.why_now: Coq's rename to Rocq (completed across 2024-2025) plus Lean 4's Mathlib reaching critical mass made proof assistants a usable industrial substrate rather than a niche. At the same time, retrieval and LLM premise selection cut the cost of the tedious step (finding the right existing lemma), which was the real barrier.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: RocqPL 2026, 'Rocq for Programming Languages', workshop at POPL 2026 (Rennes, 11-17 Jan 2026), the first under the new Rocq name; CPP 2026 (Certified Programs and Proofs) co-hosted at the same POPL. Volume signal in arXiv cs.LO week of 2026-07-22 to 07-24: 'Machine-Checked Arithmetic Bit Complexity of the Kannan-Bachem Smith Normal Form in Lean 4', 'From Dag-Like Proofs to Boolean Circuits in Lean', 'A Machine-checked Proof of Consistency for Impredicative Pure Type Systems', plus arXiv cs.PL 2026-07-17 'AoA: Theorem Proving Agent over Abstract Syntax Tree' and cs.PL 2026-07-19 'Topology in Synthetic Domain Theory and its Formalisation in Agda'.
hot_topics.one_line: Mathematics and program correctness are increasingly written in a language a computer can check line by line, and AI is now doing the tedious lemma-hunting part of that work.

hot_topics.topic: Static analysis revival: sound program facts as grounding for AI tooling
hot_topics.why_now: Two separate new static-analysis workshops appeared in the 2026 cycle at the two flagship venues, which does not happen for a settled field. The driver is that agents hallucinate about code they have not read, and call graphs, points-to sets and dataflow facts are the cheapest reliable context you can hand a model, plus the cheapest post-hoc check on what it emitted.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: TPSA 2026, 'Theory and Practice of Static Analysis', workshop at POPL 2026 (Rennes, 11-17 Jan 2026); STATIC 2026, 'Advancing Static Analysis', workshop at ICSE 2026 (Rio de Janeiro, April 2026); the long-running SOAP 2026, 'State of the Art in Program Analysis', at PLDI 2026 (Boulder, June 2026). Three distinct static-analysis workshops across POPL, PLDI and ICSE in one year. Supporting arXiv cs.PL 2026-07-17: 'A Modular Framework for Stack-Heap and Value Abstractions'; cs.SE 2026-07-23: 'Directed Symbolic Execution for Vulnerability Discovery'.
hot_topics.one_line: Old-school tools that reason about code without running it are back in fashion, because they give AI assistants facts that are actually true and catch the parts the AI made up.
hot_topics.critic_note: Confirmed on popl26.sigplan.org: TPSA 2026 (Theory and Practice of Static Analysis) is listed, Rennes, Jan 11-17 2026. Confirmed at ICSE 2026: STATIC present. Confirmed at PLDI 2026: SOAP 2026 present. So all three venues are real and correctly dated. Disqualifying: a direct survey already exists, 'A Contemporary Survey of Large Language Model Assisted Program Analysis' (2502.18474, Feb 2025), which explicitly categorizes work into static, dynamic, and hybrid, plus 'LLMs in Software Security: A Survey' (2502.07049) and practical work back to 2401.15298 (Jan 2024). The 'two NEW workshops' signal is also weaker than presented: SOAP is long-running (the claim concedes this), ICSE 2026 hosts 35 workshops including LLM4Code, so one more static-analysis workshop in a 35-workshop program is not scarcity. Unchecked: whether TPSA and STATIC are labeled first editions.

hot_topics.topic: Choreographic programming: writing one global protocol and compiling it into per-participant code
hot_topics.why_now: Distributed systems (and now multi-agent systems) are written participant by participant, so deadlocks and protocol mismatches are found in production. Choreographic projection makes those bugs unrepresentable, and the theory matured enough in 2024-2025 to get its own workshop at a flagship implementation conference rather than staying inside session-types theory.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: CP 2026, 'Choreographic Programming' workshop, co-located with PLDI 2026 (Boulder, workshops 15-16 June 2026). arXiv cs.PL 2026-07-22: 'Qoreo: Choreographic Programming for Quantum Distributed Systems'; 2026-07-16: 'Mech: Mechanised Choreographic Programming'; 2026-07-23: 'Top-down = Bottom-up: Sound and Complete Characterisations of Liveness by Multiparty Global Protocols'; 2026-07-20: 'Parameterized Verification of Deterministic MPI Programs'.
hot_topics.one_line: You write the conversation between all the participants once, as a single script, and the compiler generates each participant's code so they cannot possibly disagree about the protocol.
hot_topics.critic_note: Fails the three-year bar by roughly a decade. Confirmed on pldi26.sigplan.org/home/cp-2026: CP 2026 exists, Tuesday June 16 2026, and states no edition number. But the workshop's own page describes the field as having 'originated primarily in the context of process calculi' with 'early foundational work', a 'growing community', and an ambition to evolve CP 'into a mature paradigm'. That is maturity language written by the organizers themselves. arXiv shows 44 papers on choreographic programming spanning 2015 to 2026, earliest being Montesi's own 'Kickstarting Choreographic Programming' (1502.02519, Feb 2015), which is itself an overview paper. The claim's why_now says the theory 'matured enough in 2024-2025', which concedes maturity. A new workshop for an eleven-year-old paradigm is institutional catch-up, not a forming topic.

hot_topics.topic: Effect handlers and effect types moving from research languages into production runtimes
hot_topics.subdomain: Programming language design and type systems
hot_topics.why_now: OCaml 5 shipped effect handlers, WebAssembly's stack-switching proposal reached implementation, and Jane Street's 'Oxidized OCaml' work put modes and ownership into an industrial compiler. The open problem shifted from 'do handlers work' to how they compose with memory management, ownership and performance, which is what PLDI 2026 is now teaching as a tutorial rather than debating as a paper.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: HOPE 2026, 'Higher-Order Programming with Effects', workshop at ICFP 2026 (Indianapolis, 24-29 Aug 2026), alongside the ML Family and Haskell Symposium tracks. hot_topics.one_line: A single language feature that lets you define your own control flow (async, generators, retries, exceptions) as a library instead of begging the language designers for it, now shipping in real compilers.

hot_topics.topic: E-graphs and equality saturation as reusable optimization infrastructure
hot_topics.why_now: Equality saturation used to be a compiler-internals curiosity; the egg and egglog libraries made it a drop-in component, so it is now being applied to tensor-kernel rewriting, hardware synthesis and symbolic simplification by people who are not compiler researchers. The recent constraint is scale: e-graphs blow up in memory, and that is the live research question.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: EGRAPHS 2026, 'Equality Graphs' workshop, co-located with PLDI 2026 (Boulder, June 2026); the workshop has run annually at PLDI since 2022, which is why this is incubating rather than forming. Adjacent PLDI 2026 tutorials on the codegen side: 'ACT: End-to-End Compiler Infrastructure for Emerging AI Accelerators' and 'Writing Performance-Portable Kernels Simplified With Helion'. CGO 2026 (Sydney, 31 Jan - 4 Feb 2026, co-located with CC, PPoPP and HPCA) is the sibling venue for the code-generation half.
hot_topics.one_line: A data structure that holds every equivalent way of writing an expression at once, so a compiler can pick the fastest version instead of applying rewrite rules in a lucky order.

hot_topics.topic: Quantum software engineering and quantum programming languages
hot_topics.why_now: Error-corrected hardware roadmaps firmed up in 2024-2025, which moved the software question from toy circuit DSLs to real engineering concerns: distributed quantum programs, resource estimation, testing and debugging. This is included for map completeness, not because it is near-term employable.

hot_topics.one_line: Building the languages, type systems and testing tools that quantum computers will need, before there are quantum computers big enough to need them.

hot_topics.topic: KV-cache-centric LLM serving: inference as a storage and memory-hierarchy problem
hot_topics.subdomain: storage and file systems / distributed systems
hot_topics.why_now: Serving cost stopped being dominated by FLOPs and became dominated by moving and re-materializing attention KV state. Once prefill and decode were split across machines, the KV cache became a distributed object with a lifetime, an eviction policy and a tiering problem — i.e. a storage system, which is why storage and OS people took the problem over from ML people.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: FAST 2025 main track: 'Mooncake: Trading More Storage for Less Computation - A KVCache-centric Architecture for Serving LLM Chatbot' and 'IMPRESS: An Importance-Informed Multi-Tier Prefix KV Storage System for LLM Inference' (dblp FAST 2025). OSDI 2025 'AI + Systems' sessions incl. 'BlitzScale: Fast and Live Large Model Autoscaling with O(1) Host Caching' and 'WaferLLM: LLM Inference at Wafer Scale' (dblp OSDI 2025). Reinforced by arXiv cs.DC most-recent listing, fetched 2026-07-27 (InstantInfer, 'Keeping Cache Warm', TileSight).
hot_topics.one_line: The scratch memory a chatbot builds up while reading your prompt is now big enough and reused often enough that systems people treat it like a database to be cached, tiered and shared across machines rather than something you throw away after each request.

hot_topics.topic: Operating systems for AI agents: agent-native isolation, scheduling and revision authority
hot_topics.why_now: Agents became long-running processes that write and execute their own code against real credentials and real filesystems. The Unix process/user model has no concept of 'this program will rewrite itself and call a tool I did not authorize', so OS researchers started proposing new abstractions in 2025-2026 rather than patching sandboxes.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ASPLOS 2026 workshop program lists 'AgenticOS 2026: Operating Systems Design for AI Agents' and 'CoDAIM 2026 — 1st Workshop on Co-Design for Agentic and Multimodal AI' (asplos-conference.org/asplos2026 workshops page, fetched 2026-07-27). HotOS 2025 (dblp) ran 'Contextual Agent Security: A Policy for Every Purpose' and 'Guillotine: Hypervisors for Isolating Malicious AIs'. arXiv cs.OS most-recent listing, fetched 2026-07-27: 'Defining AI-Native Systems: Autonomy as Revision Authority', 'Hardware Mechanisms to Dynamically Throttle AI Performance'.
hot_topics.one_line: If a program can now rewrite itself and decide which tools to call, the operating system needs a way to say what it is allowed to become — not just what files it can open — and nobody has agreed on that abstraction yet.
hot_topics.critic_note: Venue evidence is clean, timeline is not. Confirmed on asplos-conference.org: 'Agentic OS: Operating Systems Design for AI Agents (AgenticOS 2026)' and 'CoDAIM 2026: 1st Workshop on Co-Design for Agentic and Multimodal AI' both appear. But the framing 'OS researchers started proposing new abstractions in 2025-2026' is off by two years: 'LLM as OS, Agents as Apps: Envisioning AIOS, Agents and the AIOS-Agent Ecosystem' (2312.03815) is from Dec 2023 and is an explicit vision/survey paper, and 'AIOS: LLM Agent Operating System' (2403.16971) is Mar 2024, with a follow-on line through Cerebrum (2503.11444) and Qualixar OS (2604.06392). Survey-grade coverage also exists: 'Toward Securing AI Agents Like Operating Systems' (2605.14932, May 2026) and 'When Agents Handle Secrets: A Survey of Confidential Computing for Agentic AI' (2605.03213). The claim's own HotOS 2025 citation shows top-venue main-track presence a year before the ASPLOS workshop. What is new is architecture-community uptake, not the topic.

hot_topics.topic: Agentic data systems: databases rebuilt as agent memory, tool surface and human-in-the-loop workflow engine
hot_topics.why_now: Agents turned out to need durable, queryable, permissioned state and a place to park intermediate results, and people kept bolting that onto Postgres or a vector store by hand. The database community's response in the 2026 cycle was to claim the problem as a data-management problem with its own consistency, provenance and access-control story.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: VLDB 2026 workshop list (vldb.org/2026/workshops.html, fetched 2026-07-27) includes two brand-new workshops with no edition number: 'ADS: Agentic Data Systems and Data-Centric AI' and 'DASHSys: Systems for Data-centric Agents with Human-in-the-loop', alongside 'Agents+Graphs' (3rd edition) and 'NOVAS: Novel Optimization for Visionary AI Systems'. arXiv cs.DB most-recent listing, fetched 2026-07-27: LLM agents for database tuning, text-to-SQL with access control, prompt management inside the DB.
hot_topics.one_line: Databases are being redesigned so an AI agent can use one as its long-term memory and its safe workspace, with permissions and an audit trail built in rather than glued on.
hot_topics.critic_note: Confirmed on vldb.org/2026/workshops.html: both ADS and DASHSys appear without edition numbers, on Friday Sept 4 2026. One correction to the claim: ADS's full title is 'The Joint Workshop on Agentic Data Systems and Data-Centric AI', a joint workshop, which weakens 'brand-new'. Disqualifying: a direct survey exists, and it makes exactly this audit's point in its title. 'A Survey of Data Agents: Emerging Paradigm or Overstated Hype?' (2510.23587, Oct 2025), with an L0-L5 autonomy taxonomy. The claim's own supporting evidence also undercuts it: Agents+Graphs is on its 3rd edition and the neighbouring AIDB is on its 7th. Note the workshop dates are Aug 31 and Sep 4 2026, both still in the future as of today, so no program content exists to inspect.

hot_topics.topic: LLMs applied to systems construction itself: verification, kernel and RTL generation, AI-driven architecture design
hot_topics.subdomain: computer architecture / operating systems / formal methods
hot_topics.why_now: Two things got cheap at once: generating a candidate proof or a candidate hardware description, and checking it automatically. That flips the economics of formal verification and design-space exploration, where the checker was always cheap and the candidate was always the expensive human part.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: 'Architecture 2.0: Workshop on AI for Computing Systems Design' runs at both ISCA 2026 (iscaconf.org/isca2026 workshops page) and ASPLOS 2026 (asplos-conference.org workshops page), both fetched 2026-07-27; ISCA 2026 also lists 'MLArchSys: Machine Learning for Computer Architecture and Systems'. HotOS 2025 (dblp): 'Can Large Language Models Verify System Software? A Case Study Using FSCQ as a Benchmark' and 'How I learned to stop worrying and love learned OS policies'. arXiv cs.AR most-recent listing, fetched 2026-07-27: 'Can AI Agents Really Complete RTL-to-GDS?', 'AlphaRoute: LLMs as Semantic Optimizers for Multi-Objective Routing', 'WaveformQA' benchmark.
hot_topics.one_line: Language models are being pointed at the hardest parts of building systems — proving an operating system correct, writing chip layouts, picking cache sizes — because a machine can now propose an answer that another machine can cheaply check.

hot_topics.topic: Vector search as a first-class systems layer: SSD-resident, updatable and hardware-accelerated ANN indexes
hot_topics.why_now: Retrieval moved from a research demo to a production dependency, so the interesting problems shifted from recall benchmarks to the boring systems ones: indexes that accept live updates without a rebuild, that spill to SSD without collapsing tail latency, and that survive a node loss.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: OSDI 2025 main track database session (dblp): 'Quake: Adaptive Indexing for Vector Search' and 'Achieving Low-Latency Graph-Based Vector Search via Aligning Best-First Search Algorithm with SSD'. FAST 2025 (dblp): 'Towards High-throughput and Low-latency Billion-scale Vector Search via CPU/GPU Collaborative Filtering and Re-ranking'. VLDB 2026 workshop list (fetched 2026-07-27) carries 'VecDB — Vector Databases, 2nd edition'. arXiv cs.AR, fetched 2026-07-27: 'D-NOVA: In-Storage Retrieval Accelerator via Dual-Bound 3D NAND-Optimized Similarity Search'.
hot_topics.one_line: Finding the nearest matching documents by meaning is now a core database service, so the work has moved to making those indexes update live, live on disk instead of RAM, and run on the storage device itself.
hot_topics.confidence_note: Mainstream, not hot-new: multiple surveys exist and OSDI/FAST give it main-track sessions. The dedicated workshop is only at its 2nd edition, which is the one 'still forming' signal here.

hot_topics.topic: Networks for AI computing: collective-communication-aware fabrics, multi-NIC GPU egress, topology co-design
hot_topics.why_now: Training and MoE inference turned the datacenter network into the critical path for a single job, not a multiplexed resource for many jobs. Congestion control and topology assumptions built for many independent flows behave badly under synchronized all-reduce and expert-routing traffic, and the failure of one link now stalls a whole cluster.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: SIGCOMM 2025 workshop program (conferences.sigcomm.org/sigcomm/2025, fetched 2026-07-27) lists NAIC, confirmed on its own CFP page as the '2nd Workshop on Networks for AI Computing', covering collective communication optimization, load balancing for distributed learning, and fault prediction/root-cause for AI fabrics. OSDI 2025 (dblp): 'Enabling Efficient GPU Communication over Multiple NICs with FuseLink'. arXiv cs.NI most-recent listing, fetched 2026-07-27: 'Fewer Paths, Better Performance: Understanding the ZCube Topology', 'MoX: Efficient MoE Routing on Direct-Connect Topologies'.
hot_topics.one_line: When thousands of GPUs must all exchange data at the same instant, the network becomes the bottleneck for one giant job rather than a shared road for many small ones, so datacenter networks are being redesigned around that traffic shape.
hot_topics.confidence_note: Attempted fetch of hoti.org/2026 (Hot Interconnects) failed with a socket hang up, so no claim is made about that venue's 2026 CFP.

hot_topics.topic: Confidential and encrypted AI: GPU trusted execution, FHE-adjacent architectures, hypervisor isolation of models
hot_topics.subdomain: systems security and confidential computing / computer architecture
hot_topics.why_now: Regulated data and third-party model weights now meet on the same accelerator, and the party who owns the data is often not the party who owns the machine. Hardware TEEs reached GPUs, and FHE hardware costs dropped enough that partial encrypted inference stopped being purely theoretical.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ISCA 2026 workshop program (iscaconf.org/isca2026, fetched 2026-07-27) lists 'SAFE AI: Workshop on Systems and Architectures For Encrypted AI' with no edition number, alongside an 'FHE & Cheddar Tutorial on Fully Homomorphic Encryption'. EuroSys 2026 day-zero program (2026.eurosys.org, fetched 2026-07-27) lists SysTEX and an S2MPC tutorial on secure multiparty computation. hot_topics.one_line: Work on running a model over data the machine's owner is never allowed to see — using hardware vaults, encrypted arithmetic, and hypervisors that treat the model itself as the untrusted party.
hot_topics.confidence_note: SAFE AI is listed without an edition number while its ISCA 2026 neighbours carry them (QCCC-26 'Fifth', 'Sixth Workshop on DRAM Security'), which reads as a first edition — but I did not fetch the workshop's own page to confirm.
hot_topics.critic_note: Oldest topic in the set by a wide margin. Confirmed on iscaconf.org/isca2026: 'SAFE AI: Workshop on Systems and Architectures For Encrypted AI' appears June 27, with no edition number, while QCCC-26 shows 'Fifth' and DRAMSec shows 'Sixth', so the claim's own confidence_note is fairly stated. But the inference does not survive: private/encrypted ML has survey coverage back to 'No Peek: A Survey of private distributed deep learning' (1812.03288, Dec 2018), covering homomorphic encryption, garbled circuits, and oblivious transfer for neural networks, plus a 2026 agent-specific survey (2605.03213). That is seven-plus years, against a three-year bar. The claim cites SysTEX at EuroSys as support, but SysTEX is a long-running series, which is evidence against forming. ISCA 2026 also lists a full FHE and Cheddar tutorial plus CPA cryptographic-acceleration tutorials at ASPLOS, which is what a settled field looks like.

hot_topics.topic: CXL memory pooling, tiered far memory, and composable disaggregated infrastructure
hot_topics.why_now: CXL-attached memory shipped in real servers, so the decade-old 'disaggregated memory' research premise finally has hardware with real, measured latency. The open questions moved from 'can we?' to the unglamorous ones: who pays the fault cost, how the OS places pages across tiers, and how to allocate a pool fairly between tenants.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: SOSP 2025 (dblp) ran a memory block with 'Oasis: Pooling PCIe Devices Over CXL to Boost Utilization', 'Scalable Far Memory: Balancing Faults and Evictions', 'Spirit: Fair Allocation of Interdependent Resources in Remote Memory Systems', and 'Demeter: Scalable and Elastic Tiered Memory for Virtualized Cloud'. OSDI 2025 (dblp): 'Tigon: A Distributed Database for a CXL Pod' and 'FineMem' fine-grained disaggregated memory management. HotOS 2025 (dblp): 'My CXL Pool Obviates Your PCIe Switch' and 'Tolerate It if You Cannot Reduce It: Handling Latency in Tiered Memory'. ASPLOS 2026 hosts 'HCDS 2026 — 5th Workshop on Heterogeneous Composable Disaggregated Systems' (fetched 2026-07-27).
hot_topics.one_line: New cabling lets a server borrow RAM from a shared pool down the rack instead of owning all of it, and the research has moved to how the operating system decides what lives in the fast local memory versus the slower borrowed kind.

hot_topics.topic: Memory-centric computing: processing-in-memory for AI, and rethinking retention guarantees for the AI era
hot_topics.why_now: The bottleneck for transformer and state-space inference is data movement between DRAM and compute, not arithmetic. Meanwhile AI workloads revealed that a lot of stored state does not actually need decade-scale durability, which reopens design space that persistent-memory orthodoxy had closed off.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: 'MCCSys — Memory-Centric Computing Systems' runs at its 5th edition at ASPLOS 2026 and again at ISCA 2026, both venue programs fetched 2026-07-27; both venues also run Ramulator/DRAM Bender memory-evaluation tutorials, and ISCA 2026 lists a 'Sixth Workshop on DRAM Security'. HotOS 2025 (dblp): 'Storage Class Memory is Dead, All Hail Managed-Retention Memory: Rethinking Memory for the AI Era'. arXiv cs.AR most-recent listing, fetched 2026-07-27: RED-PIM (attention on PIM), HEMERA (memory-centric Mamba accelerator), ADEPT and CLASP (PIM training and continual learning).
hot_topics.one_line: Because shuttling data between memory chips and processors costs more time and energy than the maths does, designers are putting small compute units inside the memory itself and relaxing how long that memory must remember things.

hot_topics.topic: Circuit-complexity characterization of transformers and chain-of-thought
hot_topics.subdomain: computational complexity / theoretical foundations of machine learning
hot_topics.why_now: The TC0 upper bound on fixed-depth transformers got sharpened in 2025-2026 into precise architecture-by-architecture results (constant vs growing precision, padding, positional encoding, average vs hard attention), so 'add a scratchpad' stopped being prompt-engineering folklore and became a theorem about what extra serial steps actually buy you. Cheap large-scale models made the empirical side testable at the same moment the proofs landed.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: NeurIPS 2025 dedicated workshop 'What Can('t) Transformers Do?', plus 'Foundations of Reasoning in Language Models' at the same meeting. 'The Expressive Power of Low Precision Softmax Transformers with (Summarized) Chain-of-Thought' (arXiv, 2026-05-18) states acceptance to ICML 2026. Concurrent cs.CC postings: 'Revisiting Padded Transformer Expressivity' (2026-05-28, constant precision = L-uniform AC0, growing precision = L-uniform TC0) and 'Average Attention Transformers and Arithmetic Circuits' (2026-05-06).
hot_topics.one_line: A fixed-depth transformer is provably no stronger than a constant-depth threshold circuit (the class TC0), which is why it cannot do certain multi-step reasoning in a single forward pass, and why chain-of-thought tokens buy it genuine extra computational power rather than merely better phrasing.

hot_topics.topic: AI as a proof-producing collaborator: autoformalization and verifier-in-the-loop theorem proving
hot_topics.why_now: A proof assistant is an incorruptible free reward signal, which is exactly what agentic search loops were missing. Once decomposition, retrieval and repair were wired around Lean/Isabelle/Rocq, competition-level benchmarks fell fast, and the theory community began asking publicly whether the same loop touches research mathematics rather than just olympiad problems.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: STOC 2026 (Salt Lake City, June 22-27) is running a first community-wide day-long workshop, 'Can AI do Theory?', on Saturday June 27, 2026, explicitly framed as a dialogue on whether AI augments or redefines TCS methodology. NeurIPS 2025 ran 'MATH-AI: The 5th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI'. Benchmark churn through 2026: miniF2F, PutnamBench, Lean-IMO-Bench, MA-ProofBench, CAM-Bench, s2n-bignum-bench, with LEAP (arXiv 2606.03303, June 2026) reporting 70% on Lean-IMO-Bench. Honest counter-signal: the LICS 2026 / FLoC 2026 affiliated workshop slate (GaLoP, LCC, TLLA, SmP, DIALOCO, ACV, IMLA, SD, WiL) contains no AI or LLM workshop, so this is forming inside the theory venues while already mainstream at ML venues.
hot_topics.one_line: Rather than trusting a language model's prose proof, you force it to emit the proof in Lean or Isabelle so a checker either accepts or rejects it, which converts mathematical reasoning into a task with a perfect automatic grader.
hot_topics.critic_note: Venue evidence is accurate but the maturity claim fails. Confirmed: STOC 2026 site lists 'Can AI do Theory?' as a day-long workshop Sat June 27, Salt Lake City, June 22-27. Confirmed: arXiv 2606.03303 is LEAP (Kung et al., 2 Jun 2026, cs.AI), abstract states 70% on Lean-IMO-Bench and all 12 Putnam 2025 problems. Disqualifying: at least three surveys already exist. 'A Survey on Deep Learning for Theorem Proving' (2404.09939, Apr 2024), 'Autoformalization in the Era of Large Language Models: A Survey' (2505.23486, May 2025), and 'Artificial Intelligence for Mathematical Reasoning: An Integrated Survey' (2606.08728, Jun 2026). The claim's own evidence concedes NeurIPS 2025 ran the FIFTH MATH-AI workshop. A topic with a two-year-old survey and a fifth-edition workshop at a top ML venue is mainstream, not forming. The honest counter-signal about LICS/FLoC is the real finding: what is new is TCS-venue uptake, not the topic.

hot_topics.topic: Strategic LLM agents, delegation, and mechanism design that survives prompt-controlled bidders
hot_topics.subdomain: algorithmic game theory and computational economics
hot_topics.why_now: Agents that actually transact went from thought experiment to shipping product across 2025-2026. That breaks a load-bearing assumption of classical mechanism design: when a human delegates to a model, the prompt is itself a strategic message and the agent becomes a second player who can misreport, so strategyproofness has to be re-proved one level up.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: EC 2026 (Rome, July 6-10, 2026) is running a first dedicated workshop, 'Game Theory and Mechanism Design with Large Language Models' (July 6, 2026), alongside 'Incentive-Based AI Alignment' and 'AI-Driven Research in EconCS' on the same day. The July 2026 arXiv cs.GT listing carries a matching cluster: 'When Is Delegated Play Truthful?', 'LLM Detection as an Intervention', 'Compensation Design', 'Compositional Semantic Communication for Physical AI', and 'The Dynamic Verifiable Multi-Agent Human Agentic Loyalty Loop'.
hot_topics.one_line: When people delegate bidding, negotiating and buying to language-model agents, the classic guarantee that honesty is your best strategy can collapse, because the prompt is a strategic message and the agent is a second player who may misreport on your behalf.
hot_topics.critic_note: Workshop exists, 'first' does not. Confirmed on ec26.sigecom.org/workshops: 'Game Theory and Mechanism Design with Large Language Models' runs July 6 2026, alongside 'Incentive-Based AI Alignment' and 'AI-Driven Research in EconCS', exactly as described. But the page carries no edition numbers for ANY of its ten workshops, so 'first dedicated workshop' is an inference from absence, not evidence. Disqualifying: surveys exist. 'LLM as a Mastermind: A Survey of Strategic Reasoning with Large Language Models' (2404.01230, Apr 2024) and 'Game-Theoretic Lens on LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems' (2601.15047, Jan 2026), which organizes the field around players, strategies, payoffs, information. Unchecked sub-item: I did not verify the individual cs.GT titles, and two of them ('Compositional Semantic Communication for Physical AI', 'The Dynamic Verifiable Multi-Agent Human Agentic Loyalty Loop') do not obviously support a mechanism-design thesis, which reads as cluster padding.

hot_topics.topic: Pseudorandom codes and cryptographically undetectable AI-output watermarking
hot_topics.why_now: Christ and Gunn's pseudorandom codes (CRYPTO 2024) converted watermarking from a heuristic token-biasing trick into a primitive with security proofs: codewords look uniformly random to anyone without the key, yet decode reliably. By 2026 the arms race is live in both directions, with public-key variants robust to edit errors on one side and published attacks that hijack the generator's PRNG on the other.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Pseudorandom codes introduced by Christ and Gunn at CRYPTO 2024 (arXiv 2402.09370). Follow-on: 'High-Rate Public-Key Pseudorandom Codes for Edit Errors' (arXiv 2605.19402, May 2026); attack paper 'Blind PRNG Hijacking: An Undetectable Integrity-Preserving Attack Against LLM Watermarking' (arXiv 2605.28632, May 2026); 'VOW: Verifiable and Oblivious Watermark Detection' (arXiv 2604.27666, Apr 2026). NeurIPS 2025 ran the 'Lock-LLM Workshop: Prevent Unauthorized Knowledge Use from Large Language Models'. Caveat on maturity: a broad survey, 'A Survey on LLM Watermarking: Theory and Deployment' (arXiv 2607.10103, July 2026), now exists, which by the survey-means-mainstream test pushes the deployment side past hot even though the PRC theory core is still incubating.
hot_topics.one_line: You can hide a signature inside AI-generated text that is provably indistinguishable from ordinary text without the secret key, so nobody can detect or strip it, yet the key holder can always prove which model produced the text.

hot_topics.topic: MicroCrypt: quantum cryptography from assumptions weaker than one-way functions
hot_topics.why_now: One-way puzzles (Khurana and Tomer, STOC 2024) gave the sub-one-way-function world a workable primitive, and 2025-2026 delivered efficient pseudorandom unitary constructions plus locality and stretch limitations. The field moved from 'is there anything down here at all' to mapping a hierarchy: which primitives imply which, and which are provably separated.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: TQC 2026 (Sherbrooke, Aug 31 - Sep 4, 2026) invited talks by Omri Shmueli (NTT Research) on quantum cryptography without secret keys and Greg Meyer (MIT) on quantum cryptography and proofs of quantumness. IACR ePrint, July 2026: 2026/1511 'Unconditional Unclonable Encryption' (Ananth, Sahai) and 2026/1509 'Efficient Unclonable Encryption from Pauli Eigenstates' (Ragavan). Named-ecosystem papers: 'A New World in the Depths of Microcrypt' (arXiv 2410.03453, Oct 2024), 'MicroCrypt Assumptions with Quantum Input Sampling and Pseudodeterminism' (arXiv 2505.14461, May 2025), 'A Note on Boosting Uncloneable Encryption in Microcrypt' (arXiv 2605.27647, May 2026), 'On the Limits of Stretching Quantum Pseudorandomness' (arXiv 2606.24736, June 2026). Pseudorandom states trace to Ji, Liu and Song, CRYPTO 2018.
hot_topics.one_line: Quantum physics may let you build encryption, signatures and unclonable ciphertexts even in a hypothetical world where the one-way functions that all classical cryptography rests on simply do not exist.

hot_topics.topic: Refutation of the polynomial-time low-degree conjecture and the future of statistical-computational gaps
hot_topics.subdomain: computational complexity / theoretical foundations of machine learning
hot_topics.why_now: The low-degree method was the workhorse for arguing that planted statistical problems are computationally hard, and its polynomial-time formalization was the load-bearing assumption behind sharp threshold claims for community detection, sparse PCA and tensor PCA. A preprint five days old at time of writing claims that formalization is false, which reopens what counts as evidence of average-case hardness.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: arXiv 2607.20318, 'The Polynomial-Time Low-Degree Conjecture is False', posted 2026-07-22 in cs.CC. The conjecture it targets is the [MW23] formalization used, for example, by 'Low degree conjecture implies sharp computational thresholds in stochastic block model' (arXiv 2502.15024, ETH Zurich, Feb 2025). Confidence caveat: this is a single unrefereed preprint less than a week old and has not yet been vetted by the community; treat the refutation as claimed rather than settled.
hot_topics.one_line: For years theorists used a shortcut called the low-degree method to argue that certain statistical estimation problems are computationally hard, and a July 2026 preprint claims the polynomial-time version of that shortcut is outright false.

hot_topics.topic: Post-quantum migration at internet scale: crypto-agility, hybrid deployment, and the harvest-now-decrypt-later clock
hot_topics.why_now: With ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA standardized and HQC added as a code-based backup for algorithm diversity, the open problem stopped being 'which scheme' and became 'how do you swap cryptography out of a billion deployed systems'. 2026 measurement work shows the gap plainly: roughly half of surveyed domains negotiate hybrid key exchange while essentially none deploy hybrid certificates.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: CRYPTO 2026 (Santa Barbara, Aug 17-20, 2026) affiliated events on Aug 15-16 include CLAW (Cryptography Lattices Algebra Workshop) and WAC8 (8th Workshop on Attacks in Cryptography), alongside ITC, CFAIL and PPML. The July 2026 arXiv cs.CR listing carries an internet-scale TLS readiness measurement over 32,011 domains (49.3% hybrid KEM support, 0% hybrid certificates), 'SoK: Post-Quantum Cryptography Implementation in Software', 'Classical Acceptance Is Not Hybrid Authentication' on X.509 verifier semantics across seven codebases, 'An Assessment Framework for Cryptographic Agility', and several LLM-assisted PQC code-migration papers.
hot_topics.one_line: The world is replacing RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography with lattice- and code-based schemes before quantum computers exist, because traffic captured and stored today can be decrypted later once they do.

hot_topics.topic: Range avoidance and the meta-complexity route to explicit constructions
hot_topics.why_now: Range avoidance became the single bottleneck connecting circuit lower bounds, explicit combinatorial constructions and derandomization after it was used to prove that symmetric exponential time requires near-maximum circuit size. Since then it has absorbed proof complexity generators, cell-probe lower bounds and Kolmogorov-complexity characterizations of cryptographic primitives.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: arXiv comments across this line name STOC, FOCS and ITCS. Papers: 'Symmetric Exponential Time Requires Near-Maximum Circuit Size' (2023) and its 2026 successor 'Near-Maximum Circuit Lower Bounds for Exponential Time with Merlin-Arthur Queries' (arXiv, 2026-07-10); 'Hardness of Range Avoidance and Proof Complexity Generators from Demi-Bits' (2025-11-18); 'A Note on Avoid vs MCSP' (2025-12-25); 'Downward self-reducibility in the total function polynomial hierarchy', placing Avoid in UEOPL^NP (2025-07-25); 'Cell-Probe Lower Bounds via Semi-Random CSP Refutation' (2025-07-29). On the meta-complexity side, 'A Meta-Complexity Characterization of Minimal Quantum Cryptography' (2025-10-09) characterizes EFI pairs via Kolmogorov-style measures.
hot_topics.one_line: Range avoidance asks you to name any string that a given circuit can never output, and it turns out that solving it efficiently would hand you explicit constructions of objects (rigid matrices, hard truth tables) that mathematicians have failed to write down for decades.

hot_topics.topic: Quantum LDPC codes and constant-overhead fault tolerance under real hardware constraints
hot_topics.subdomain: quantum computing theory / coding theory and error correction
hot_topics.why_now: Asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes were proved to exist, so the frontier shifted from existence to the constraints real machines impose: bounded-degree qubit connectivity, single-shot and correlated-error decoding, and decoders that must finish inside a syndrome cycle. That is a coding-theory-meets-systems problem rather than a pure asymptotics problem.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: FOCS 2026 (New York, Nov 8-11, 2026, co-located with TCC 2026) accepted 'Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation with Adversarial Errors' among its 310 papers. arXiv 2603.24588, 'Finite-Degree Quantum LDPC Codes Reaching the Gilbert-Varshamov Bound' (2026-03-25), is the most-engaged paper in this cluster on alphaXiv (30 votes, 290 views). arXiv 2605.01035, 'A Scalable FPGA Architecture for Real-Time Decoding of Quantum LDPC Codes' (2026-05-01), covers the decoder-latency side; arXiv 2607.20421 (2026-07-22) studies the glassy energy landscape of the classical LDPC codes underlying good qLDPC constructions.
hot_topics.one_line: Quantum error correction used to cost roughly a thousand physical qubits per useful logical qubit, and new quantum LDPC codes cut that overhead by about an order of magnitude, provided you can decode them fast enough on real hardware.

hot_topics.topic: Learning-augmented algorithms (algorithms with predictions) beyond online problems
hot_topics.why_now: The pattern (consistency when the prediction is good, robustness to the classical worst case when it is wrong) is settled for online problems, so 2026 pushed it into places it had not reached: exact exponential-time algorithms, approximation for NP-hard selection, and even warm-starting problems governed by fine-grained complexity conjectures such as cubic-time all-pairs shortest paths.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: The ALPS community bibliography 'Algorithms with Predictions' at algorithms-with-predictions.github.io is the field's standing index. The Antoniadis et al. ICLR 2025 framework for predictions in NP-hard selection is extended by 'Learning-Augmented Approximation for Unrelated-Machines Makespan Scheduling' (arXiv 2606.13133, June 2026). New territory in 2026: 'Learning Augmented Exact Exponential Algorithms' (arXiv 2606.18807, 2026-06-17), 'Warm-Starting All-Pairs Shortest Paths with Predictions' (arXiv 2607.00857, 2026-07-01), 'Learning-Augmented Online Minimization with Dual Predictions' (arXiv 2606.05380), 'Learning-Augmented Algorithms for Online Vertex Cover' (arXiv 2606.22831). NeurIPS 2025 also ran 'Differentiable Learning of Combinatorial Algorithms: From Theory To Practice'.
hot_topics.one_line: You let a machine-learned prediction steer a classical algorithm, but you design it so a good prediction makes it fast while a wrong prediction still cannot make it worse than the ordinary worst-case guarantee.

hot_topics.topic: Coupled AI Earth-system emulation (learned models growing past the atmosphere into waves, snow, ocean and sea ice)
hot_topics.subdomain: climate modelling and AI Earth-system emulation
hot_topics.why_now: AI medium-range weather forecasting is a settled operational fact, so the frontier moved to the cheap part: adding an extra Earth-system component to a learned model costs a training run, while adding it to a physics model costs a decade of code. The 2025-2026 releases are about coupling, not headline forecast scores.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ECMWF AIFS blog (fetched 2026-07-27): 'AIFS v2 adds snow fields' (26 Nov 2025) describing ML Earth-system modelling across land, ocean, hydrology, sea ice and waves; 'data-driven ocean wave modelling for the AIFS' (21 Aug 2025); first ensemble AIFS (21 Jun 2024); AIFS training adapted for IFS Cycle 50r1 (12 May 2026).
hot_topics.one_line: Weather-forecasting neural networks that learned the atmosphere are now being trained to carry the ocean, snow and sea ice too, turning a forecast model into a whole-planet emulator.

hot_topics.topic: Observation-native, grid-free atmospheric world models (train on raw observations instead of reanalysis)
hot_topics.subdomain: climate modelling and AI Earth-system emulation
hot_topics.why_now: Every current AI forecast model is trained on reanalysis, which is itself a physics-model product that is expensive, lagged and grid-locked. Making the learned model consume raw satellite and station observations directly removes the last dependency on the thing it was supposed to replace.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: 'Earth-o1: A Grid-free Observation-native Atmospheric World Model', arXiv 2605.06337 (7 May 2026), retrieved via alphaXiv 2026-07-27. There is no dedicated main-track session or special issue for this yet; the closest standing host is the climate-emulation strand of the NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning' (San Diego, 7 Dec 2025). LOW-CONFIDENCE ADDITION, not fetched: I recall a Nature 2025 end-to-end observation-to-forecast paper (Aardvark Weather); treat as unverified until checked.
hot_topics.one_line: Instead of learning from a cleaned-up model reconstruction of past weather, these models learn straight from the messy raw satellite and station measurements.
hot_topics.critic_note: The claim's own low-confidence addition is the decisive evidence against it: 'Aardvark Weather: end-to-end data-driven weather forecasting' is arXiv 2404.00411, submitted 30 Mar 2024, so learning forecasts directly from raw observations rather than reanalysis is over two years old and reached a top journal. Earth-o1 is real (2605.06337, 7 May 2026, Gong et al., 25 authors). Venue evidence is vague by the rubric and by the claim's own admission: no dedicated session or special issue, only the climate-emulation strand of 'Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning', which is on both the verified neurips.cc/virtual/2024 and 2025 lists and has run since 2019. A survey also covers the neighbourhood: 'Foundation Models for Weather and Climate Data Understanding: A Comprehensive Survey' (2312.03014, Dec 2023). Not three years hot, but the venue evidence does not carry a forming claim.

hot_topics.topic: Geospatial foundation models and the benchmark/embedding layer built around them
hot_topics.why_now: Petabytes of free Sentinel/Landsat imagery plus self-supervised pretraining made a general-purpose satellite encoder feasible, and the bottleneck shifted from training one to comparing them: shared embeddings and benchmark suites are now the contested ground.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: EarthVision workshop at CVPR 2025 (Nashville, 11 Jun 2025) lists 'Foundation models and representation learning in the context of EO' in its CfP and ran a challenge on compressing EO data into 1024-dimensional embeddings for downstream evaluation (grss-ieee.org, fetched 2026-07-27). hot_topics.one_line: One large pretrained model turns any satellite image into a reusable numeric fingerprint, so mapping floods, crops or deforestation becomes a small fine-tune instead of a new project.

hot_topics.topic: Generative (diffusion) downscaling and regional climate model emulation
hot_topics.why_now: Adaptation decisions need kilometre-scale climate, but running physics at that scale for a century is unaffordable. Diffusion models became good enough to add fine detail while preserving the joint structure between variables, which older statistical downscaling destroyed and which compound risk (heat plus drought, rain plus surge) depends on.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Dense 2026 preprint cluster retrieved via alphaXiv 2026-07-27: 'IPSL-AID: Generative Diffusion Models for Climate Downscaling' (arXiv 2604.03275, Mar 2026); 'Regional Climate Model Emulation with Diffusion Approaches: What is the Added Value of Generative Machine Learning?' (arXiv 2606.14570, Jun 2026); 'Generative climate downscaling enables high-resolution compound risk assessment by preserving multivariate dependencies' (arXiv 2605.11531, May 2026). The physics-side rival is funded and operational: EU Destination Earth digital twins (Climate Change Adaptation; Weather-Induced Extremes), Phase 3 started July 2026 (destination-earth.eu, fetched 2026-07-27), alongside 'Global kilometer-scale climate simulations' with the 2.6 km ARP-GEM model (arXiv 2607.16125, Jul 2026).
hot_topics.one_line: Image-generation models are being used to sharpen coarse climate projections into street-scale maps, which is why the argument is now about whether the added detail is real or invented.

hot_topics.why_now: Interconnection queues, not chips, became the binding constraint on AI capacity in 2025-2026, and the response is to stop treating a data centre as fixed demand: if inference can be deferred or shifted, the load becomes a grid resource and gets connected faster.

hot_topics.topic: Silicon sampling: LLMs as synthetic survey respondents and experimental subjects, and the validity backlash against it
hot_topics.why_now: Running a 2,000-person survey or lab experiment used to cost tens of thousands of dollars and months of IRB and recruitment; prompting a model to produce 2,000 personas now costs a few dollars and an afternoon. hot_topics.topic: Valid statistical inference from machine-generated measurements: prediction-powered inference (PPI) and design-based supervised learning (DSL)
hot_topics.why_now: Social scientists now routinely have an LLM label a million documents for 'is this speech populist?' and then run a regression on those labels. The labels are cheap but biased, and plugging them straight into a regression silently corrupts the coefficient and the confidence interval. The fix is a small human-labelled subset used to de-bias the large machine-labelled set, and 2024-2026 was when that fix hardened into a standard toolkit.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Method comparison and synthesis papers verified via Consensus this session: Audinet de Pieuchon et al. (2025) 'Benchmarking Debiasing Methods for LLM-based Parameter Estimates', comparing DSL against PPI in finite samples; Emmenegger et al. (2026) 'Prediction-Powered Inference Across Many Tasks for AI Evaluation & Social Science Research', with a case study auditing language models on election information during the 2024 US presidential election; Song et al. (2026) 'Demystifying Prediction Powered Inference', an explicit synthesis-plus-decision-flowchart paper. The existence of that synthesis paper is itself the maturity signal. hot_topics.one_line: If you let an AI label your data and then compute a statistic from those labels, the statistic is wrong in a predictable direction, and these methods use a small hand-checked sample to correct it back to something you can honestly report.

hot_topics.topic: Mechanism design for markets where AI agents transact on behalf of humans (agentic commerce, delegated bidding, LLM matching markets)
hot_topics.why_now: Classical mechanism design assumes a rational agent with a fixed utility function reporting a preference. An LLM acting under delegation is none of those things: it is prompt-sensitive, its 'preferences' are not stable, and it can be steered by the seller's text. Once real money started moving through agent checkout in 2025-2026, the question of whether strategyproofness and stable matching survive contact with LLM agents became an empirical question, not a thought experiment.

hot_topics.topic: Algorithmic monoculture: correlated screening decisions when every firm buys the same model
hot_topics.why_now: Hiring, lending, and admissions screening consolidated onto a handful of vendors, and then onto a handful of foundation models underneath those vendors. The consequence is systemic rather than individual: a candidate rejected by one screener is now correlated-rejected everywhere, so the same people are locked out of the whole market at once. That is a different harm from 'the model is biased', and it needed its own theory, which arrived in 2025-2026.
