Origin citation from my own knowledge, NOT verified by fetch this session: Kleinberg & Raghavan, 'Algorithmic monoculture and social welfare', PNAS 2021.
hot_topics.one_line: If every employer screens applicants with the same underlying model, rejection stops being a series of independent coin flips and becomes one verdict applied everywhere, which is worse for the rejected than ordinary bias.

hot_topics.topic: AI persuasion and AI-mediated depolarization: chatbots that measurably change political and factual beliefs
hot_topics.why_now: Two decades of persuasion research concluded that durable attitude change is very hard and that debunking barely works. Conversational models broke that finding: a personalized, evidence-citing, patient interlocutor is now available at zero marginal cost, and the measured effects survive months. That flips the research question from 'can anything change minds?' to 'who is allowed to deploy the thing that does, and at what scale?'
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Verified 2026 arXiv cluster: 'AI systems out-persuade expert humans' (2606.16475, 2026-06-15, the highest-engagement paper in this cluster at 22 votes / 95 views on alphaXiv); 'Artificial intelligence can persuade people to take political actions' (2604.09200, 2026-04-10); 'Synthetic Contact with AI Reduces Cross-Partisan Animosity' (2607.02181, 2026-07-02); 'Brief chatbot interactions produce lasting changes in human moral values' (2604.21430); 'Perceived Political Bias in LLMs Reduces Persuasive Abilities' (2602.18092). The adjacent human-intervention literature has already reached meta-analysis, verified via Scholar Gateway: Stasielowicz, L. (2025), 'The Effectiveness of Interventions Addressing Conspiracy Beliefs: A Meta-Analysis', European Journal of Social Psychology 56(1), 275-291, published 08 December 2025. Seed paper from my own knowledge, NOT verified by fetch this session: Costello, Pennycook & Rand, 'Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI', Science 2024.
hot_topics.one_line: Short conversations with a chatbot durably move people's conspiracy beliefs, partisan hostility, and even moral judgements, which is simultaneously the most promising and the most alarming finding in political psychology right now.

hot_topics.topic: Foundation models of cognition: fitting one large model to hundreds of psychology experiments instead of one model per task
hot_topics.why_now: Cognitive science historically built a bespoke small model per paradigm (one for risky choice, one for bandit learning, one for memory). Large transformers fine-tuned on aggregated human trial-level data can now out-predict those bespoke models across many paradigms at once, which forces the field to ask what a model that predicts everything but explains nothing is actually for. That is a genuine theory crisis, not a benchmark race.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Named NeurIPS 2025 workshops, verified from the neurips.cc/virtual/2025/events/workshop listing of 56 workshops: 'CogInterp: Interpreting Cognition in Deep Learning Models' (explicitly framed around using cognitive science, psychology and linguistics to understand how a model performs or learns a task) and 'Data on the Brain and Mind'. Discipline venue: CogSci 2026, Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society, Rio de Janeiro, 22-25 July 2026, theme 'Cognitive (In)Efficiency' (verified on cognitivesciencesociety.org). Verified 2026 arXiv work: 'Using Cognitive Models to Improve Language Model Simulation of Human Persuasion Games' (2606.17657); 'NeuroCogMap Reveals Cognitive Organization of Large Language Models' (2607.00397); 'Divergent Minds, Convergent Baselines: A Bounded-Rationality Account of LLM-Human Strategic Behaviour' (2605.26437). Landmark from my own knowledge, NOT verified by fetch this session: Binz et al., 'Centaur', a foundation model of human cognition, Nature 2025.
hot_topics.one_line: Instead of a separate hand-built theory for each type of psychology experiment, researchers are training one big neural network on all of them, and it predicts people better while explaining them less.

hot_topics.topic: Industrialized replication: reproduction as standing infrastructure rather than occasional scandal
hot_topics.why_now: The 2010s replication crisis produced diagnosis but no machinery. What changed is that reproduction became a routinized, staffed, funded pipeline with its own organizations, events, and publication channel, so re-checking a paper is now a normal career activity rather than an act of aggression. Cheap compute plus mandatory data-and-code deposit made bulk re-execution feasible.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Institute for Replication (I4R), verified on i4replication.org as of July 2026: 232+ discussion papers documenting reproduction and replication attempts, 132+ fellows, a global programme of 'replication games', a replication-tools curation effort, and a podcast titled 'Allegedly Does Not Replicate'; July 2026 blog output on data and code availability failures and on coding errors in published research. Conference series: Metascience 2027, 14-16 June 2027, Montreal, presented jointly by the Neuro Tanenbaum Open Science Institute and the Center for Open Science (verified on metascience.info), continuing the Metascience conference series. NOTE: my fetch of the American Sociological Association meeting pages returned HTTP 403 twice, so I am making no claim about ASA programming here.
hot_topics.one_line: Checking whether a published social-science result actually holds up has been turned into an organized, staffed, continuously running operation instead of a once-a-decade crisis.

hot_topics.topic: Task-level measurement of AI's effect on work, replacing job-count forecasting
hot_topics.subdomain: labour economics and the economics of AI
hot_topics.why_now: Predictions about 'jobs lost to AI' were unfalsifiable because occupations are bundles of tasks and only some tasks move. What became newly available is direct observation of which tasks people actually bring to AI systems, at national scale, published under open licence, which lets labour economists work at task granularity instead of occupation granularity for the first time.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Anthropic Economic Index, verified live via its own tooling this session: publisher Anthropic, licence CC BY 4.0, latest data period 2026-05-01, snapshot modified 2026-06-24, covering 121 countries with a published usage index, 51 US states, 22 job categories and 923 tracked occupations of which 718 have published usage; headline global split 51.38 percent augmentation versus 48.62 percent automation conversation style, and 43.36 percent work / 40.20 percent personal / 16.45 percent coursework use case split. Landing page https://www.anthropic.com/economic-index. Verified July 2026 arXiv econ.GN cluster (fetched from arxiv.org/list/econ.GN/2026-07): 'AI Adoption in S&P 500 Firms'; 'Experimental Evidence on the Learning Impact of Generative AI'; 'The Economic Benefits and Costs of AI and Policies to Mitigate AI's Impact on Inequality' (Jackson & Kanik); 'Robots and the Public Finance of Disability Insurance'. Management venue: AOM 2026, the 86th Academy of Management Annual Meeting, 31 July - 4 August 2026, Philadelphia (verified on aom.org; no published theme statement found on the page I fetched). IMPORTANT CAVEAT carried from the data publisher itself: this index measures observed usage matched to job tasks, not who the users are, and it explicitly cannot support displacement or job-security conclusions.
hot_topics.one_line: Rather than guessing which jobs AI will eliminate, economists now measure which specific work tasks people actually hand to AI, and whether they stay involved or hand the whole thing over.

hot_topics.topic: Cognitive offloading, deskilling, and the productivity illusion in human-AI collaboration
hot_topics.why_now: The first wave of AI-at-work studies measured output speed and found large gains. The second wave started measuring what happens to the human: whether people can tell when offloading helps, whether they retain the skill, and whether the felt speedup matches the measured one. Enough people have now used these tools daily for two or three years that longer-horizon skill effects are finally measurable rather than speculative.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: CogSci 2026, Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society, Rio de Janeiro, 22-25 July 2026, whose stated theme is 'Cognitive (In)Efficiency', framed in the programme materials as: 'Many behaviors and mental processes are not a product of this ideal of efficiency and often deviate from it' (verified on cognitivesciencesociety.org). Verified arXiv work: 'Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction' (2605.23177, 2026-05-22), which asks directly whether users know when to offload; 'Cognitive Trajectory Modeling: Quantifying Human-AI Co-Creation' (2606.15358). From the verified July 2026 arxiv.org/list/cs.CY/2026-07 listing: 'AI usage patterns are shaped by perceived gains in human agency'; 'The Double-edged Effect of Banning Generative AI on Online Q&A Communities'; 'CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education'; 'Beyond Detection: Redesigning Assessment and Governance of Generative AI at UPM'.
hot_topics.one_line: People routinely feel faster when working with AI than they measurably are, and researchers are now testing whether handing thinking to a model quietly erodes the underlying skill.
hot_topics.critic_note: Fails the survey test. A review-journal article already covers this exact framing: Kim, Usman, Garvey & Duhachek (2025), 'From algorithm aversion to AI dependence: Deskilling, upskilling, and emerging addictions in the GenAI age', Consumer Psychology Review 9(1) 142-164, published 3 December 2025 (Consumer Psychology Review publishes reviews only). Also Daniel, Msambwa & Wen (2025), 'Can Generative AI Revolutionise Academic Skills Development in Higher Education? A Systematic Literature Review', European Journal of Education 60(1), 14 February 2025. Empirical work continues through Farhat (2026), 'When AI Thinks for Us: Unveiling the Cognitive and Social Toll of ChatGPT Over-Reliance', Applied Cognitive Psychology, 23 April 2026. That is at least 18 months of published review-level attention. The venue evidence is also weaker than presented: I verified CogSci 2026 (22-25 July 2026, Sheraton Grand Rio, Rio de Janeiro, theme 'cognitive (in)efficiency'), but the theme statement on the page frames suboptimality in communication and social coordination generally and does not name AI, offloading, or deskilling, and no symposium, workshop, or tutorial on this topic is listed. A general conference theme is not a session on the topic. The arXiv anchor is real and strong: 2605.23177 'Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction' (Yu, Cheng, Jabbar, Sucholutsky, Collins, Jurafsky, Hawkins, 2026-05-22) verified, as is 2606.15358 (full title 'Cognitive Trajectory Modeling: Quantifying Human-AI Co-Creation through Cognitively Grounded Interaction Trajectories', Davis, 2026-06-13). The specific speedup-illusion measurement may be new; the topic as scoped is not.

hot_topics.topic: Algorithmic collusion and the regulation of AI pricing
hot_topics.why_now: Pricing algorithms were shown in simulation to learn supracompetitive prices without any communication, which is collusion that no existing antitrust doctrine handles, because doctrine requires proof of agreement. What is new is the shift from simulation to identified empirical settings and to concrete regulatory instruments such as mandated disclosure, which is what competition authorities actually need.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Verified July 2026 arXiv econ.GN and econ.TH listings (fetched directly): 'Strategic Information Disclosure in Algorithmic Pricing' (Wang & Ye), which frames the regulatory question as an information-design problem, also indexed as arXiv 2607.04345, 2026-07-05; 'Shared Bidding Algorithms and Competition: Evidence from Electricity Markets' (Eschenbaum), an identified empirical setting rather than a simulation; 'When Pricing Agents Meet Buying Agents: Personalized Pricing and Verifiable Trust' (2607.16343, 2026-07-16). Home venue: ACM EC'26, 27th ACM Conference on Economics and Computation, Rome, 6-10 July 2026. Foundational citation from my own knowledge, NOT verified by fetch this session: Calvano, Calzolari, Denicolò & Pastorello, 'Artificial intelligence, algorithmic pricing, and collusion', American Economic Review 2020.
hot_topics.one_line: Pricing bots can learn to keep prices high without ever talking to each other, which is illegal in effect but not under any law as currently written, so economists are designing rules that would catch it.

hot_topics.topic: AI Virtual Cell: predicting unseen perturbation responses
hot_topics.why_now: Pooled CRISPR screens read out by single-cell sequencing (Perturb-seq) got cheap enough to produce million-cell perturbation atlases, so the field's question moved from 'can we embed a cell' to 'can we predict a perturbation nobody ran'. The 2026 turn is adversarial: benchmark and negative-result papers are now arriving alongside the models, and several report that generic tabular or linear baselines match specialized single-cell foundation models.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'AI Virtual Cells and Instruments: A New Era in Drug Discovery and Development' (verbatim from neurips.cc/virtual/2025 workshop list); ICLR 2026 workshop 'Learning Meaningful Representations of Life (LMRL)', scoped to virtual cells; bioRxiv 2026-07-02, Palla, Hillsley, Kim, Royer, 'Tabular Foundation Models Are Competitive Cellular Perturbation Predictors Across Biological Scales' (DOI 10.64898/2026.06.28.735106); alphaXiv 2026-04-30 'Benchmarking virtual cell models for in-the-wild perturbation response' (2604.27646) and 2026-05-11 'AssayBench: An Assay-Level Virtual Cell Benchmark for LLMs and Agents' (2605.10876).
hot_topics.one_line: Train a model on enough single-cell measurements that you can ask 'what happens to this cell type if I knock out gene X' and get a usable answer without running the experiment.

hot_topics.topic: Closed-loop AI agents driving wet-lab experiments
hot_topics.why_now: Tool-using LLM agents matured at the same time as biofoundry robotics and cheap DNA synthesis, so the bottleneck moved from proposing a hypothesis to closing the loop: agent proposes, robot executes, result re-enters the agent's context. This is a 2026 framing, not a settled research programme.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ICLR 2026 workshop 'Machine Learning for Genomics Explorations (MLGenX)' carries the explicit 2026 theme 'From Reasoning to Experimentation: Closing the Loop Between AI Agents and the Biological Lab' (iclr.cc/virtual/2026 workshop listing); bioRxiv 2026-07-08, Tassinari et al., 'Barcoded-Plasmid DNA library construction for recording cell lineage trees enabled by a Scalable and modular Biofoundry-based Automated Robotic Pipeline' (DOI 10.64898/2026.07.07.736956); alphaXiv 2026-06-01 'AgentPLM: Agentic Protein Language Models with Reasoning-Augmented Decoding for Protein Sequence Design' (2606.02386).
hot_topics.one_line: An LLM agent picks the next experiment, a lab robot runs it, and the measured result feeds straight back into the next proposal with no human in the loop.
hot_topics.critic_note: A survey already exists on the agentic version specifically: 'Agentic AI for Self-Driving Laboratories in Soft Matter: Taxonomy, Benchmarks, and Open Challenges' (2601.17920, 25 Jan 2026). The underlying field runs from 'Self-driving laboratory for accelerated discovery of thin-film materials' (1906.05398, Jun 2019), through a review at 2304.03272 (Apr 2023), 'Agents for self-driving laboratories applied to quantum computing' (2412.07978, Dec 2024), 'The Evolving Role of Programming and LLMs in the Development of Self-Driving Laboratories' (2504.13870, Mar 2025), and a perspective at 2603.05526 (Feb 2026). MLGenX does appear in the verified iclr.cc/virtual/2026 list, but it is a recurring series rather than a new venue, and I did not verify the quoted 2026 theme text. Seven years for self-driving labs, and the agentic framing already has its taxonomy paper.

hot_topics.topic: Biosecurity safeguards for generative biology
hot_topics.why_now: Open-weight genome foundation models and de novo protein design tools got good enough that DNA-synthesis order screening, which works by matching against databases of known hazardous sequences, can be evaded by designed sequences that share no homology with anything catalogued. Screening now has to work on sequences that have never existed.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'Biosecurity Safeguards for Generative AI' (verbatim from neurips.cc/virtual/2025 list; carries no edition number, unlike sibling workshops explicitly marked '2nd'/'Second', which is consistent with a first edition); alphaXiv 2026-07-15 'Screening of Biosecurity Features in Metagenomic Data with Evo 2 Probes' (2607.14070); 2026-06-09 'ABC-Bench: An Agentic Bio-Capabilities Benchmark for Biosecurity' (2606.11150); 2026-05-10 'The Biosecurity Blind Spot: Systematic Dual-use Detection in Open Science Infrastructure' (2605.28843).
hot_topics.one_line: If a model can design a protein nobody has ever seen, the safety checks that compare DNA orders against lists of known dangerous sequences stop working, so people are building screens that judge what a sequence would do rather than what it resembles.

hot_topics.topic: Bespoke, mutation-specific in vivo genome editing (N-of-1 therapies)
hot_topics.why_now: Base and prime editors plus lipid-nanoparticle and engineered-AAV delivery made it technically feasible to build an editor against one patient's exact mutation on a months-long timescale. The remaining constraints are regulatory pathway, manufacturing and cost, not molecular biology, which is why the 2026 literature is dominated by platform and policy framing rather than new chemistry.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Nature Biomedical Engineering 2025 (vol 10, issue 5, pp 952-967), Alves, Kleinstiver, Musolino et al., 'Treatment of a severe vascular disease using a bespoke CRISPR-Cas9 base editor in mice' (DOI 10.1038/s41551-025-01499-1, PubMed PMID 40935887); Pediatric Research, 2026-07-17, 'The future of pediatric gene therapy: CRISPR-Cas9, AI, and personalized medicine' (DOI 10.1038/s41390-026-05270-3, PubMed PMID 42469418). Retrieved via PubMed.
hot_topics.one_line: Rather than one drug per disease, you engineer a gene editor against one patient's specific mutation and dose them within months.

hot_topics.topic: Genome language models and generative genomics
hot_topics.why_now: DNA foundation models can now be trained and sampled at whole-genome scale, so the field has shifted from scoring existing variants to writing new regulatory elements and genome segments. The live question is validation: whether a generated sequence actually functions when put in a cell, which is exactly what the 2026 workshop title flags as a 'barrier'.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ICLR 2026 workshop 'Generative AI in Genomics (Gen2): Barriers and Frontiers' (iclr.cc/virtual/2026 list; scoped to directed evolution in protein science and engineering cellular states); ICLR 2026 workshop 'Machine Learning for Genomics Explorations (MLGenX)'; bioRxiv 2026-06-23, Merchant, Hie et al., 'A high-level programming language for generative biology with Proto' (DOI 10.64898/2026.06.22.733870); bioRxiv 2026-06-30 'AI-enabled rhodopsin design for blue-light enhanced bacterial growth' (DOI 10.64898/2026.06.29.735265).
hot_topics.one_line: Language models trained on DNA rather than text, used to write new gene-regulatory sequences and genome segments that are then tested in living cells.

hot_topics.topic: Integration of unpaired spatial multi-omics
hot_topics.why_now: Spatial platforms became cheap and multiplexed enough that most labs now hold several modalities (transcriptome, protein, chromatin) measured on adjacent but not identical tissue sections, with no principled way to fuse them. The methods problem is unpaired alignment, not measurement.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ISMB 2026 (ISCB, Washington DC, 12-16 July 2026) runs dedicated COSI tracks where this work lands, including RegSys, Function, CompMS and NetBio, from 21 COSIs listed on the ISCB programme page; bioRxiv 2026-07-02, Cai and Li, 'SpatialFuser: a unified framework for integrative analysis of unpaired spatial multi-omics data' (DOI 10.1101/2025.09.14.676067); bioRxiv 2026-07-02 'SpaGRD deciphers signaling architectures in spatial transcriptomics using graph reaction-diffusion systems' (DOI 10.64898/2026.06.28.735031). PubMed returns 126 spatial-omics atlas/benchmark papers in Nature-family journals and Cell since 2025, which is the volume signature of a mainstream field.
hot_topics.one_line: Measure genes, proteins and chromatin in the same piece of tissue while tracking where each cell physically sits, then stitch those separately-collected measurements into one map.

hot_topics.topic: Synapse-resolution connectomics linked to recorded function
hot_topics.why_now: Electron-microscopy reconstruction pipelines completed a whole fly brain and a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex with matched functional recordings of the same neurons. The field's open question inverted: it is no longer whether a wiring diagram can be obtained, but what a wiring diagram is actually good for predicting.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: PubMed returns 105 papers since September 2024 with 'connectome' or 'connectomics' in the title tied to electron microscopy, MICrONS or FlyWire, published across the Nature family, which is mainstream volume; on the modelling side, NeurIPS 2025 hosted 'Data on the Brain and Mind' and 'Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations' (both verbatim from the neurips.cc/virtual/2025 workshop list). Note: mammalian-scale connectomics is much earlier than invertebrate; the mainstream label reflects the field as a whole.
hot_topics.one_line: Slice a brain, image every synapse, rebuild the complete wiring diagram, and then check that diagram against recordings of what those exact neurons were doing while the animal was alive.

hot_topics.topic: Foundation models for brain and body biosignals
hot_topics.why_now: Large public EEG, iEEG and wearable-physiology corpora plus standard transformer pretraining recipes made cross-subject and cross-dataset transfer feasible, where previously essentially every brain-computer-interface decoder had to be trained per subject and often per session. Amortising calibration is the whole prize.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'Foundation Models for the Brain and Body Workshop', scoped to 'large-scale, pretrained AI systems designed to learn from biosignals' including EEG and neural interfaces (verbatim from neurips.cc/virtual/2025 list; carries no edition number, consistent with a first edition); NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'Learning from Time-Series for Health', covering physiological signals and EHR time series; NeurIPS 2025 'Recent Advances in Time Series Foundation Models: Have We Reached the BERT Moment?' supplies the sceptical counterweight.
hot_topics.one_line: One pretrained model for brain and body signals that works on a new person without being retrained from scratch, the way a language model works on text it has never seen.
hot_topics.critic_note: Three surveys already exist: 'A Simple Review of EEG Foundation Models: Datasets, Advancements and Future Perspectives' (2504.20069, Apr 2025), 'EEG Foundation Models: A Critical Review of Current Progress and Future Directions' (2507.11783, Jul 2025), and 'Foundation Models for Cross-Domain EEG Analysis Application: A Survey' (2508.15716, Aug 2025), plus a consolidation benchmark, EEG-FM-Bench (2508.17742, Aug 2025). The line starts at Neuro-GPT (2311.03764, Nov 2023) and runs to 77 title matches. The venue claim itself is fine: 'Foundation Models for the Brain and Body Workshop' is verbatim in the neurips.cc/virtual/2025 list and has no counterpart in the 2024 list. But a subfield that produced three surveys and a benchmark before its first workshop is consolidating, not forming.

hot_topics.topic: Ambient clinical AI and the evidence standards catching up to it
hot_topics.why_now: Speech-to-note LLM scribes were deployed across health systems in 2024-2025 well ahead of any controlled evidence that they save clinician time. Randomised pragmatic trials embedded in the EHR are only now being registered, and in parallel the field is arguing about what counts as evidence in clinical-AI fairness audits, where a null subgroup result may just mean the study was underpowered.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: medRxiv 2026-07-13, Wieben et al., 'Protocol for an EHR-embedded pragmatic randomized control trial of Ambient AI to Reduce Nursing Staff Documentation Time' (DOI 10.64898/2026.07.09.26357653); medRxiv 2026-07-13, Stark and Ritter with ADNI, 'From Fairness Findings to Fairness Claims: An Evidence Classification Scheme for Clinical AI' (DOI 10.64898/2026.07.09.26357666); NeurIPS 2025 'The Second Workshop on GenAI for Health: Potential, Trust, and Policy Compliance' (verbatim from the neurips.cc/virtual/2025 list, explicitly a second edition).
hot_topics.one_line: LLMs that listen to a clinical visit and write the note, now finally being put through randomised trials to check whether they actually save anyone time.

hot_topics.topic: Surveillance-bias-adjusted spatial epidemiology
hot_topics.why_now: Routine pathogen genomic sequencing and wastewater monitoring became standing infrastructure after COVID, but the resulting data are systematically biased by who gets tested and where. The 2026 methodological turn is to model the ascertainment process explicitly and then externally validate the corrected risk map against an independent disease, rather than assuming complete case ascertainment.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ISMB 2026 (ISCB, Washington DC, 12-16 July 2026) programme lists a dedicated 'Pathogen Data Network Forum' special session alongside the MICROBIOME and CAMDA COSI tracks; medRxiv 2026-07-13, Ma, Zhang and Lin, 'Surveillance-adjusted syphilis risk mapping across U.S. counties: a Bayesian spatial analysis with external validation against HIV and gonorrhea outcomes' (DOI 10.64898/2026.07.09.26357652) and, same authors and date, 'Shared respiratory infectious disease hotspots identify priority countries for pandemic preparedness: a Bayesian spatiotemporal analysis with COVID-19 external validation' (DOI 10.64898/2026.07.09.26357662).
hot_topics.one_line: Disease maps that correct for the fact that some places test far more than others, then prove the correction worked by predicting a different disease they were not fitted on.

hot_topics.topic: Perspectivism: annotator disagreement treated as signal rather than noise
hot_topics.why_now: LLMs made bulk annotation cheap, which moved the bottleneck from 'can we label enough data' to 'whose label counts as correct' — and majority-vote gold standards visibly destroy the variation that pragmatics, toxicity, and stance judgments are actually made of.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: NLPerspectives: The 4th Workshop on Perspectivist Approaches to Natural Language Processing, EMNLP 2025 (fetched from 2025.emnlp.org workshop list). Related: UncertaiNLP, the Second Workshop on Uncertainty-Aware NLP, EMNLP 2025.
hot_topics.one_line: Instead of forcing human annotators into one 'right' answer, this line of work keeps their disagreement in the dataset and treats the spread of opinions as the thing to model.

hot_topics.topic: LLM-as-judge relevance assessment inside official IR evaluation infrastructure
hot_topics.why_now: Generative answers broke the Cranfield assumption that a fixed pool of documents can be human-judged once and reused; NIST responded by standing up tracks where the automatic judge itself is the object of study rather than a convenience.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: TREC 2025/2026 track list at trec.nist.gov (fetched): AutoJudge, Million LLM, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), RAGTIME (RAG TREC Instrument for Multilingual Evaluation), User Simulation, Change Detection, Video Question Answering. AutoJudge, Million LLM and RAGTIME are recent additions to a track roster that historically changed slowly.
hot_topics.one_line: The US government's benchmark programme for search now runs official tracks on whether an AI model can stand in for the human who decides if a search result was any good.
hot_topics.critic_note: Fails the survey test decisively and the three-year test. At least three surveys predate this claim by roughly 20 months: 'A Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge' (2411.15594, 2024-11-23, 172 votes, 18k views), 'LLMs-as-Judges: A Comprehensive Survey on LLM-based Evaluation Methods' (2412.05579, 2024-12-07), 'From Generation to Judgment: Opportunities and Challenges of LLM-as-a-judge' (2411.16594, 2024-11-25). The IR-specific relevance-judgment line is also mature: 'Judging the Judges: A Collection of LLM-Generated Relevance Judgements' (2502.13908, 2025-02-19, authored across Amsterdam, Waterloo, UCL, Microsoft, Amazon, Padua), 'Benchmarking LLM-based Relevance Judgment Methods' (2504.12558, 2025-04-17), 'Revisiting Human-vs-LLM judgments using the TREC Podcast Track' (2601.05603, 2026-01-09). The TREC evidence itself is real: trec.nist.gov lists AutoJudge, Change Detection, Million LLM, RAG, RAGTIME, User Simulation, and Video QA, and registration for TREC 2026 is open. But official NIST tracks are the mainstreaming of a topic, not its formation. Unchecked sub-point: the page does not state inception years for any track, so 'recent additions to a roster that historically changed slowly' is unverified. The verdict does not depend on it.

hot_topics.topic: Locating classical linguistic categories as circuits inside language models
hot_topics.why_now: Circuit-level interpretability tooling matured to the point where a specific grammatical feature (animacy, agreement, argument structure) can be traced to identifiable components, so century-old category debates in linguistics now have a mechanistic test bed.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: BlackboxNLP 2025: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP, EMNLP 2025 (seven proceedings volumes in the ACL Anthology). Current example from arXiv cs.CL, July 2026: 'Where Animacy Lives in Large Language Models: Tracing the Circuits of the Animacy Concept'; also 'What, Where, and How: Disentangling the Roles of Task, Language, and Model in Code Model Representations'.
hot_topics.one_line: Researchers open up a language model and try to find the exact internal machinery that handles a grammatical distinction such as living-versus-nonliving nouns.

hot_topics.topic: Epistemic regress arguments against autonomous self-correction in AI agents
hot_topics.subdomain: epistemology / philosophy of mind and action
hot_topics.why_now: Self-critique, reflection and self-verification loops became a default engineering pattern in agent systems, and philosophers moved in to ask whether a system checking its own output can ever terminate the justification chain without an outside source.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: PhilSci-Archive deposit, July 2026: Lee-Sursin, Julian & Ryoo, Hong Joo, 'A Regress Argument Concerning Autonomous Self-Correction in AI Agents' (fetched from philsci-archive.pitt.edu latest deposits). Adjacent framing in CRCL 2024 special issue: Sarah Lawsky, 'Computational Law and Epistemic Trespassing'. Caveat: preprint-level evidence, no journal special issue confirmed this session.
hot_topics.one_line: If an AI agent grades and fixes its own work, philosophers argue you get an infinite regress, because the check needs a check, and nothing inside the system ever grounds it.
hot_topics.critic_note: The deposit is real: I confirmed on philsci-archive.pitt.edu/cgi/latest that Lee-Sursin & Ryoo (2026), 'A Regress Argument Concerning Autonomous Self-Correction in AI Agents' is listed, and no other AI-self-correction deposits appear alongside it. But this fails the vague-venue default. There is no venue at all: one unrefereed preprint by authors with no established standing in this debate, and the claim itself concedes no journal or special issue. The supporting citation does not support the topic: Lawsky's 'Computational Law and Epistemic Trespassing' is about experts overstepping domain boundaries, a different concept from justificatory regress, so it is padding rather than corroboration. Separately, the substantive claim is not new. The empirical finding that intrinsic self-correction fails without an external signal already has a critical survey: 'When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs' (2406.01297, 2024-08-19, UIUC and Penn State), plus 'Internal Consistency and Self-Feedback in Large Language Models: A Survey' (2407.14507, 2024-09-18), and a continuing stream through 2026 (2601.00828, 2604.22273, 2606.23196). What is new here is philosophical vocabulary over a two-year-old, already-surveyed result. One paper is a paper, not a forming field.

hot_topics.topic: GPU-accelerated first-order methods for large-scale linear and conic programming (PDLP, cuPDLP, HPR-LP)
hot_topics.why_now: Linear programming was owned for 40 years by simplex and interior-point methods, both bound to sparse matrix factorization, which parallelizes badly. Restarted primal-dual hybrid gradient is matrix-free (only matrix-vector products), so it maps onto GPUs. Between 2023 and 2026 this went from a proof of concept to production tooling: cuPDLP.jl (2023), cuPDLP-C (2024), cuPDLPx and HPR-LP (2025), then presolving and distributed multi-GPU D-PDLP (2026). What got cheap is solving LPs with tens of millions of variables without a factorization.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'GPU-Accelerated and Scalable Optimization (ScaleOpt)', first edition (verified from neurips.cc/virtual/2025 workshop listing). Survey: 'An Overview of GPU-based First-Order Methods for Linear Programming and Extensions', arXiv:2506.02174, June 2025 (Univ. of Chicago, MIT). Active 2026 follow-ups: D-PDLP arXiv:2601.07628 (Jan 2026), 'Presolving for GPU-Accelerated First-Order LP Solvers' arXiv:2604.23951 (Apr 2026).
hot_topics.one_line: Instead of solving huge planning problems by factorizing a giant matrix, you use a simple iterative method that only multiplies vectors, which lets a GPU do it and makes previously impossible problem sizes routine.

hot_topics.topic: Decision-focused learning with generative scenario models (contextual stochastic optimization)
hot_topics.why_now: The old pipeline was predict, then optimize, with the predictor trained on forecast accuracy that nobody actually cares about. Two things unblocked the end-to-end version: differentiable optimization layers plus new solver-free training objectives removed the need to backpropagate through a solver on every step, and conditional generative models (diffusion, flow matching) became good enough to serve as the scenario generator feeding the optimizer. The 2026 frontier is decision-dependent uncertainty, where your decision changes the distribution you face.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'ML x OR: Mathematical Foundations and Operational Integration of Machine Learning for Uncertainty-Aware Decision-Making', first edition, and NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'Differentiable Learning of Combinatorial Algorithms: From Theory To Practice' (both verified from neurips.cc/virtual/2025). Note on maturity: the base paradigm already has surveys ('Decision-Focused Learning: Foundations, State of the Art, Benchmark and Future Opportunities', arXiv:2307.13565, 2023; 'A Survey of Contextual Optimization Methods for Decision Making under Uncertainty', arXiv:2306.10374, 2024), so the base is mainstream. What is new is the generative branch: Diffusion-DFL arXiv:2510.11590 (Oct 2025), 'Decision-Weighted Flow Matching for Contextual Stochastic Optimization' arXiv:2606.16790 (Jun 2026), 'A Solver-Free Training Method for Predict-then-Optimize' arXiv:2606.19587 (Jun 2026).
hot_topics.one_line: Train the forecasting model to make the downstream decision good rather than to make the forecast accurate, because a small prediction error in the wrong place can wreck a schedule while a large one elsewhere costs nothing.

hot_topics.topic: Randomized and mixed-precision numerical linear algebra as default infrastructure, with dynamical low-rank approximation as the moving edge
hot_topics.subdomain: numerical analysis and numerical linear algebra
hot_topics.why_now: GPU tensor cores made low precision (FP16, FP8) an order of magnitude cheaper than FP64, and sketching made low-rank factorizations cost a single pass over the data. Both are now packaged, not just published: RandLAPACK-style libraries and new releases such as librla (arXiv:2607.20732, July 2026) put them in reach of non-specialists. The genuinely unsettled part is grafting sketching onto dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) for large matrix differential equations and kinetic PDEs, where the low-rank factors must evolve in time while preserving positivity and conservation.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Two Acta Numerica surveys anchor the mainstream status: Martinsson and Tropp, 'Randomized numerical linear algebra: Foundations and algorithms', Acta Numerica 29 (2020); Higham and Mary, 'Mixed precision algorithms in numerical linear algebra', Acta Numerica 31 (2022). hot_topics.one_line: Use deliberate randomness and deliberately sloppy arithmetic to compress and solve enormous linear algebra problems, with error bounds proving the sloppiness is safe.

hot_topics.topic: Geometric and structure-preserving methods in scientific machine learning
hot_topics.why_now: Neural surrogates for physical systems were fast but silently violated conservation of energy, mass, positivity and symplectic structure, so long rollouts drifted or blew up. The fix is to bake the geometry into the architecture (symplectic and port-Hamiltonian layers, Lie group structure, positivity corrections) rather than hoping the loss function enforces it. This is now a distinct research programme rather than a trick, and classical geometric integration theory turns out to supply the analysis.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Oberwolfach workshop 2632b, 'Geometric Methods in Scientific Machine Learning', MFO, 2 to 7 August 2026 (verified from mfo.de workshop schedule). Related named venues: NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations'; ICLR 2026 workshop 'Geometry-grounded Representation Learning and Generative Modeling'; NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'Non-Euclidean Foundation Models and Geometric Learning'. hot_topics.one_line: Build the physics conservation laws into the shape of the neural network itself, so a learned simulator cannot invent energy even when it is wrong about the details.

hot_topics.topic: PDE foundation models and error-controlled neural operator surrogates
hot_topics.why_now: Neural operators (DeepONet, Fourier neural operator) are already mainstream as methods, but they shipped without error bars, which blocks them from engineering and inverse-problem use where a wrong answer is expensive. Two things changed in 2025 and 2026: conformal prediction gave a distribution-free way to attach calibrated uncertainty to an operator surrogate, and randomized training removed the expensive nonconvex fit. In parallel, the ambition moved from one network per equation to a single model covering families of PDEs, which is why the field is now getting its own dedicated venues.

hot_topics.one_line: Train one network to act as a reusable solver across a whole family of physics equations, and attach an honest confidence interval so engineers can actually trust the output.
hot_topics.critic_note: Venue evidence is real: 'AI&PDE: ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI and Partial Differential Equations' and 'The 2nd Workshop on Foundation Models for Science' both appear verbatim in the iclr.cc/virtual/2026 workshop list, 'AI4Physics' in icml.cc/virtual/2026, 'Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences' in neurips.cc/virtual/2025, and arXiv 2606.29440 exists (PCA-RaNN, submitted 28 Jun 2026). hot_topics.topic: Constrained and preference-aligned optimal transport for generative sampling (Schrodinger bridges, flow matching)
hot_topics.why_now: Flow matching made continuous-time transport the default recipe for generative models, which promoted optimal transport from an elegant theory to the working language of systems people ship. The open problem is that real deployments need the transport to respect hard constraints (physical feasibility, safety sets, budget) and soft preferences, and classical OT theory has no clean account of a constrained coupling learned from preference data. Wasserstein gradient flow and Schrodinger bridge machinery is being retooled to supply it.

hot_topics.one_line: Generative models work by learning the cheapest way to morph noise into data, and the live question is how to force that morphing to stay inside hard real-world constraints.

hot_topics.topic: Information-theoretic LLM provenance: multi-bit watermarking as a coding and hypothesis-testing problem
hot_topics.why_now: Watermarking shipped in production (Google's SynthID-Text) and transparency regulation turned provenance from a research curiosity into a compliance requirement. That immediately exposed the limit of single-bit detection, which only answers whether text is machine-generated. The demand is now multi-bit: embed which model, which user, which session, and survive editing. That is exactly a noisy-channel coding problem with a false-positive constraint, so error-correcting codes, soft LLR decoding and Neyman-Pearson detection theory moved in.

hot_topics.topic: Semantic and goal-oriented communication, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC)
hot_topics.why_now: Shannon deliberately declared meaning irrelevant to communication. That was the right call when the receiver was a human, and the wrong call when the receiver is a machine that only needs enough information to take one correct action. Cheap neural codecs made transmit-the-meaning-not-the-bits implementable, and 6G standardization made ISAC (one waveform doing radar sensing and data transfer at once) a required feature rather than a paper topic. The mathematics that is missing is a rate-distortion theory where distortion is measured in downstream task loss.

hot_topics.topic: Learned certificates for control: neural Lyapunov functions and control barrier functions with formal verification
hot_topics.why_now: A Lyapunov function proves a controller will not diverge and a barrier function proves it will not leave a safe set, but for decades nobody could construct them for high-dimensional nonlinear systems. You can now learn them as neural networks. The reason this became credible rather than decorative is that SMT and MILP verifiers got fast enough to formally certify small networks, so a learned certificate can arrive with a proof attached instead of a convergence plot. The unsolved part is scaling verification past toy network sizes.

hot_topics.topic: Distribution-free uncertainty quantification for multi-step agentic pipelines (conformal prediction, e-values, sequential testing)
hot_topics.why_now: Conformal prediction is mature as a statistical technique, but it assumes one prediction from one exchangeable stream. Agent systems chain many stochastic steps with feedback, so errors compound and the exchangeability assumption breaks, which makes a single average accuracy number close to meaningless. The demand that is new is per-decision, composable guarantees under sequential and adaptive querying, which is pushing e-values, anytime-valid inference and drift monitoring into what used to be a pure statistics corner.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ICML 2026 workshop 'Statistical Frameworks for Uncertainty in Agentic Systems', first edition (verified from icml.cc/virtual/2026). ICML 2026 'The 2nd Workshop on Epistemic Intelligence in Machine Learning' and 'ICML 2026 Hypothesis Testing Workshop' (both verified, same listing). ICLR 2026 workshop 'Catch, Adapt, and Operate: Monitoring ML Models Under Drift' (verified from iclr.cc/virtual/2026). NeurIPS 2025 workshop 'Reliable ML from Unreliable Data'. Standing venue for the base technique is COPA, the Symposium on Conformal and Probabilistic Prediction. Note: conformal prediction itself is mainstream and well surveyed; the agentic and sequential branch is the forming part.
hot_topics.one_line: Attach a statistically guaranteed error rate to each individual decision an AI system makes, and keep that guarantee valid when hundreds of those decisions are chained together.

hot_topics.topic: AI-generated counterexamples to long-standing Erdos-type conjectures
hot_topics.why_now: In 2026 an AI system produced a genuine counterexample to the Erdos planar unit-distance conjecture, and unlike prior 'AI found a better bound' results it was short enough to be human-verified. That single event triggered a chain: mathematicians re-read adjacent conjectures with the new construction idea and knocked over several more within eight weeks. What got cheap is not proof search but adversarial construction search over algebraic parameter families, and the outputs are small enough to check by hand.

Follow-on wave: arXiv 2605.28781, 'The sum-product conjecture is false for real numbers' (2026-05-27), a human disproof of Erdos-Szemeredi explicitly credited to inspiration from the unit-distance result; arXiv 2606.16738, counterexample to the near-quadratic Elekes-Ronyai expander conjecture (2026-06-15); arXiv 2607.20525, 'Autonomous disproofs of the sum-product conjecture over R with GPT-5.5 Pro' (2026-07-09). Venue layer: AITP 2026, 11th Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Theorem Proving, Aussois, 30 Aug - 4 Sep 2026, invited talk by Robert Veroff, 'Automating the search for proofs of open conjectures'.
hot_topics.one_line: AI systems have started producing real counterexamples that overturn decades-old conjectures in combinatorics, and because the counterexamples are short, humans can check them and then reuse the trick on neighbouring problems.

hot_topics.topic: The Jacobian conjecture falls in dimension three, and the Keller-map literature reboots
hot_topics.why_now: An explicit degree-seven polynomial map from C^3 to C^3 with constant nonzero Jacobian determinant but no global inverse was exhibited in July 2026, killing an 87-year-old conjecture in dimension 3 and above. Everything downstream that quietly assumed the conjecture is now in play: people are re-deriving which Keller-map behaviours are actually possible, and the two-dimensional case is suddenly the interesting frontier rather than a warm-up.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Terence Tao's blog, 'A digestion of the Jacobian conjecture counterexample' (2026-07-21), which states the explicit map, verifies the Jacobian is the constant -2, and exhibits three points with the same image. Corroborating July 2026 cluster on arXiv math.AG: 'Graded Keller maps and the Jacobian Conjecture', counterexamples in characteristic 2 and in five variables, arXiv 2607.21572 'Generic degrees of real polynomial Keller maps with non-dense image' (2026-07-23), plus spillover arXiv 2607.18186 'Small Counterexamples to the Gaussian Moments Conjecture' (2026-07-20) and arXiv 2607.18166 on non-injective field redefinitions in scalar QFT (2026-07-20). CAVEAT: Tao's post attributes the discovery to an AI system; I verified the mathematics is circulating and the literature wave is real, but I did not independently verify the attribution and it rests on one source.
hot_topics.one_line: A polynomial map can have a constant nonzero Jacobian determinant and still fail to be invertible, which mathematicians had believed impossible since 1939, and the July 2026 counterexample has reopened an entire corner of algebra.

hot_topics.topic: Theory-scale autoformalization: translating whole papers and theories into Lean, not single statements
hot_topics.why_now: Statement-level autoformalization plateaued as a research problem once type-correctness climbed from roughly 53% to 76% in two years, and the field noticed that a formalisation effort is inherently theory-level: hundreds of interdependent definitions, not one isolated theorem. Multi-agent pipelines with a compiler in the loop made whole-paper translation tractable in 2026, and the target moved from 'does it compile' to 'is it a faithful statement of what the paper actually claimed'.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Dense June-July 2026 arXiv cluster: 2607.13292 'Theory-Level Autoformalization: From Isolated Statements to Unified Formal Knowledge Bases' (2026-07-14), 2606.26525 'Theory-Scale Auto-Formalization of Logics for Computer Science' (2026-06-25), 2606.31134 'Beyond the Library: An Agentic Framework for Autoformalizing Research Mathematics' (2026-06-30), 2607.20503 'LeanFlow: A Case Study in Workflow-Driven Lean Autoformalization', 2607.11307 'Efficient Test-Time Optimization for Multi-Agent Proof Autoformalization' (2026-07-13). Venue layer: AITP 2026 invited talk by Auguste Poiroux (EPFL), '(Auto-)Formalization of the Fields Medal Sphere Packing Results'; Lean community blog, 'Sphere Packing Project, Post 1' (2026-03-02, Birkbeck / Hariharan / Lee) on recent autoformalisation; CPP 2026 (Rennes, 12-13 Jan 2026, co-located with POPL 2026) accepted 'Higher order differential calculus in Mathlib' and 'A Certifying Proof Assistant for Synthetic Mathematics in Lean'.
hot_topics.one_line: Instead of asking a model to formalise one theorem, teams now point agent pipelines at an entire paper or theory and have the proof assistant's compiler check the whole dependency graph.

hot_topics.topic: Flagship human formalisation programs: Fermat's Last Theorem, class field theory, sphere packing in Lean/mathlib
hot_topics.why_now: These are the first formalisation efforts aimed at genuinely modern research mathematics rather than nineteenth-century results, and they are funded, staffed and managed like software projects with blueprints, dependency graphs and reviewer training. They matter as infrastructure: once class field theory and the Langlands prerequisites are in mathlib, the marginal cost of formalising the next arithmetic-geometry paper drops sharply, which is precisely what makes the autoformalization wave above viable.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Fermat's Last Theorem formalisation project, directed by Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, funded by EPSRC grant EP/Y022904/1, with public blueprint and GitHub repository (imperialcollegelondon.github.io/FLT). Lean community blog milestones: Class Field Theory formalisation with a Clay Mathematics Institute workshop in July 2025; Grothendieck abelian categories with injectives; the Freyd-Mitchell theorem; affine group schemes and Hopf algebras (Toric project); 'Mathlib Reviewer Bootcamp 2026', Stockholm (blog post 2026-04-25) as evidence the bottleneck has shifted from authors to reviewers.
hot_topics.one_line: Large teams are rewriting landmark modern proofs, including Fermat's Last Theorem, in a language a computer can check line by line, and the real product is the reusable library underneath.

hot_topics.topic: Benchmarks and evaluation design for machine mathematics
hot_topics.why_now: Competition-problem scores saturated, so the measurement problem moved to harder ground: constructive combinatorics where you must exhibit an object rather than verify one, and faithfulness of formal statements rather than mere compilation. A headline number like type-correctness hides which error classes a method actually fixed, so the 2026 work is about error stratification and about benchmarks that cannot be gamed by pattern-matching a known proof.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: MATH-AI, the 5th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI, co-located with NeurIPS 2025, San Diego, 6 December 2025, with benchmark design an explicit listed topic (series began at ICLR 2021, then NeurIPS 2022, 2023, 2024). arXiv 2606.10479 'ComBench: A Benchmark for Rigorous Proof Reasoning and Constructive Realization in Olympiad-Level Combinatorics' (2026-06-09); arXiv 2606.31002 'Beyond Compilation: Evaluating Faithful Natural-Language-to-Lean Statement Formalization' (2026-06-30); arXiv 2606.28013 'The Signal-Coverage Matrix: Stratifying Type and Semantic Errors in Statement Autoformalization' (2026-06-26), which reports type-correctness rising from about 53% to about 76% in two years and argues the scalar conceals what each method fixed; arXiv 2606.14867 'Evaluating the Robustness of Proof Autoformalization in Lean 4' (2026-06-12).
hot_topics.one_line: Now that models ace competition problems, the open question is how to measure mathematical ability honestly, which pushed the field toward benchmarks requiring you to construct an object and toward checking whether a formal statement really says what the English said.

hot_topics.topic: Human-AI collaborative proof workflows and the auditability debate
hot_topics.subdomain: research practice and philosophy of proof
hot_topics.why_now: Fully autonomous provers turned out to be the wrong shape for research: a mathematician wants a collaborator that proposes lemmas mid-argument, not an oracle that answers a fixed proposition. Simultaneously, AI systems started contributing results nobody had verified in advance, which turned 'who checks this' from a philosophical question into an operational one, with formal machine-checkable output proposed as the audit layer.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: arXiv 2607.14582 'MathCoPilot: An Interactive System for Human-AI Symbiotic Paradigm of Mathematical Research' (2026-07-16), explicitly arguing against the autonomous-agent framing; arXiv 2606.02484 'Iteris: Agentic Research Loops for Computational Mathematics' (2026-06-01); arXiv 2607.17388 'Mathematical Discovery in the Wild: AI-Guided Proofs in Banach Space Theory' (2026-07-19), five new results generated by AI and then human-verified; arXiv 2607.06377 'Automation Without Understanding' by Jun-Yong Park (2026-07-07), which cites the 2026 AI disproof of the Erdos unit-distance conjecture and proposes requiring AI systems to emit decision-critical claims in machine-checkable form. Venue layer: AITP 2026 invited talks by Simon Frieder (Oxford, 'AIMO and all that') and Christian Szegedy (AletheAI).
hot_topics.one_line: The interesting systems are no longer the ones that prove a stated theorem alone but the ones that sit alongside a mathematician mid-argument, which forces a new question about who is accountable for checking machine-produced mathematics.
hot_topics.critic_note: MathCoPilot verifies exactly (arXiv 2607.14582, 16 July 2026) but it is not the leading edge, it is a late entrant to an argument already won. The collaborator-not-oracle position was made earlier and with far more attention: 2602.10177 'Towards Autonomous Mathematics Research' (2026-02-10, 115 votes), 2603.26524 'Mathematical methods and human thought in the age of AI' (2026-03-27, 108 votes), and above all 2605.06651 'AI co-mathematician: Accelerating mathematicians with agentic AI' (2026-05-07, 105 votes), a workbench for interactive open-ended research, which is the claim's thesis two months early and with a hundred times the engagement. Also 2604.16347 'Lean Atlas: An Integrated Proof Environment for Scalable Human-AI Collaborative Formalization' (2026-03-16), which additionally raises the exact auditability point that a type checker guarantees logical correctness but not faithfulness, and 2606.04273 'Characterizing initial human-AI proof formalization workflows' (2026-06-02). Both a survey (2606.08728, 2026-06-07) and a textbook ('Lectures on AI for Mathematics', 2604.11504, 2026-04-13) already exist. Not checked: 2607.17388, 2607.06377, the AITP 2026 invited talks, and the asserted 2026 AI disproof of the Erdos unit-distance conjecture.

hot_topics.topic: The categorical local Langlands conjecture after the geometric Langlands proof
hot_topics.subdomain: number theory, arithmetic geometry and representation theory
hot_topics.why_now: The unramified geometric Langlands conjecture was proved (Gaitsgory-Raskin and collaborators), which freed the community to attack the categorical local statement of Fargues-Scholze. The machinery that made this possible, derived stacks and ind-coherent sheaves in the condensed setting, only stabilised in the last few years, and 2026 saw the first full program document reducing the general case to proper Levi subgroups.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: arXiv 2606.00983, David Hansen and Lucas Mann, 'The categorical local Langlands conjecture' (submitted 2026-05-31, revised 2026-06-04), a 266-page program spanning number theory, algebraic geometry and representation theory; it proves the full CLLC for GL_n conditional on one compatibility hypothesis and gives an induction principle for classical groups. Companion expository signal: arXiv 2605.23167, 'What is the Geometric Langlands Correspondence about?' (2026-05-22), written explicitly because the recent unramified GLC proof 'attracted a lot of publicity'.
hot_topics.one_line: A deep dictionary translating between number theory and geometry was proved in one setting, and the frontier has moved to restating and proving it as an equivalence of categories over the p-adic numbers.

hot_topics.topic: Higher category theory as working infrastructure for geometry and representation theory
hot_topics.why_now: Stable infinity-categories and condensed/analytic methods stopped being a specialist dialect and became the ambient language of several neighbouring fields, so the 2026 activity is diffusion rather than foundation-laying: surveys aimed at representation theorists, and workshop programs organised around the transfer itself. Higher semiadditivity and ambidexterity are the genuinely new technical layer on top.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: Oberwolfach (MFO) workshop 'Higher Category Theory in Geometry and Representation Theory', 16-21 August 2026, is the clearest institutional signal that the transfer is the topic. arXiv 2603.14970 'Stable infinity-categories for representation theorists' (2026-03-16, unusually high engagement at 19 votes and 181 views on alphaXiv) is an explicit invitation to a neighbouring field. New technical layer: arXiv 2607.07431 'Higher Semiadditive Character Theory' (2026-07-08), generalising T(n)-local monoidal and K(t)-local transchromatic character theory; arXiv 2605.05195 'Stable homotopy theory of higher categories' (2026-05-06). Infrastructure co-signal: Clausen-Scholze condensed mathematics notes posted to arXiv in May 2026 as declared stable citable versions (2605.03658 'Lectures on Condensed Mathematics', 2605.11731 'Condensed Mathematics and Complex Geometry'), which is what a framework does when it stops moving and starts being cited.
hot_topics.one_line: A very abstract bookkeeping language for spaces and algebra has become the default working vocabulary in algebraic geometry and representation theory, so the current effort is teaching it sideways to those fields rather than developing it further.

hot_topics.topic: Quantum topology, skein theory and character varieties in low dimensions
hot_topics.why_now: Quantum invariants of knots and three-manifolds, hyperbolic geometry, cluster algebras and categorification converged enough that a single organising framework, skein theory, now spans all four, and institutions are betting a full semester on the convergence. The practical hook is that skein relations give a diagrammatic, almost combinatorial entry point to questions about smooth structures on four-manifolds and mapping class group representations.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: IPAM long program 'Quantum Topology, Character Varieties and Low-Dimensional Geometry', UCLA, 23 September - 18 December 2026, organised by Daniel Douglas (Virginia Tech), Ko Honda (UCLA), David Jordan (Edinburgh), Effie Kalfagianni (Michigan State), Aaron Lauda (USC), Ian Le (ANU), Jessica Purcell (Monash) and Paul Wedrich (Hamburg). The program is explicitly structured around four streams: character varieties and their quantum deformations; hyperbolic geometry and quantum invariants; contact geometry and cluster algebras; and categorification in quantum topology.
hot_topics.one_line: Invariants of knots that came out of mathematical physics are being connected to the hyperbolic geometry and smooth structure of three- and four-dimensional spaces, with knot diagrams and a small set of local relations as the shared computational language.

hot_topics.topic: o-minimality and tame geometry meeting complex analytic geometry
hot_topics.why_now: Model theory's tameness notions became a working tool in Hodge theory and arithmetic geometry over the last several years, but the transfer stalled at the sheaf-theoretic level: almost nothing was known about coherent cohomology or vector bundle classification in the definable setting, even for curves. 2026 work is filling exactly that gap, which is what turns a borrowed technique into a genuine subject.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: arXiv 2607.08052 'Complex curves in o-minimal geometry' (2026-07-09), which states there has been 'considerable progress relating o-minimality to complex analytic geometry' yet 'almost nothing is known about coherent cohomology or the classification of vector bundles, even for curves'. Adjacent model-theory activity: arXiv 2512.06386 'Model theory of tame valued fields and beyond: recent developments and open questions' (2025-12-06); arXiv 2605.18123 'Fractional Helly property and combinatorics of forking in NTP_2 theories' (2026-05-18), importing a combinatorial geometry property into classification theory. CONFIDENCE CAVEAT: evidence here is arXiv-only. I found no dedicated named workshop or special issue for this thread, and the arXiv math.LO recent listing I scraped was dominated by modal logic, categorical logic and choiceless set theory rather than tame geometry, so the maturity rating is my judgement rather than a venue reading.
hot_topics.one_line: A branch of logic that studies shapes definable without pathological wiggling turned out to be the right setting for hard problems in complex and arithmetic geometry, and researchers are now building the missing sheaf and bundle theory inside it.

hot_topics.topic: RL post-training of vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies
hot_topics.why_now: Imitation-pretrained VLA base models are now commodity starting points (arXiv July 2026 describes a 100k-hour real-robot corpus, Xiaomi-Robotics-1), so the open problem moved from 'can we train one' to 'how do we improve one after pretraining'. The verifiable-reward RL recipe that worked for LLM reasoning is being ported to action policies, and fast learned simulators make the rollouts affordable.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: RSS 2026 (Sydney, July 13-17) accepted workshop list includes 'Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models (RL4VLA)' and 'Post-training for Robotics Foundation Models', both first editions (fetched from roboticsconference.org/program/workshops). Precursor: CVPR 2025 'Workshop on 3D-LLM/VLA: Bridging Language, Vision and Action in 3D Environments'. arXiv all:'vision-language-action' returned 40 papers spanning only 2026-07-14 to 2026-07-23.
hot_topics.one_line: Robots now start from a big pretrained model that turns camera images plus an instruction into motor commands, and the hot question is how to keep improving that model with trial-and-error reward instead of more human demonstrations.
hot_topics.critic_note: Venue evidence is fully accurate: roboticsconference.org/program/workshops confirms RSS 2026 in Sydney, 13-17 July 2026, with 'Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models (RL4VLA)' (#28) and 'Post-training for Robotics Foundation Models' (#7), verbatim. Overstated on maturity. Three VLA surveys already cover post-training as a section: 2509.19012 'Pure Vision Language Action (VLA) Models: A Comprehensive Survey' (2025-09-23), 2510.07077 'Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotics: A Review' (2025-10-08), 2512.11362 'An Anatomy of Vision-Language-Action Models' (2025-12-12), plus 2607.06706 (2026-07-07). RL post-training specifically has been high-attention since 2509.09674 'SimpleVLA-RL' (2025-09-11, 198 votes, 4348 views) and 2510.06710 'RLinf-VLA' (2025-10-08, 76 votes), with production frameworks through 2026 (RL-VLA3, WoVR, VLA-OPD, EXPO-FT). Internal inconsistency worth naming: the claim treats '40 papers in nine days' as evidence of forming, but in the conformal prediction entry it treats exactly that volume signature as proof a method is settled. Two dedicated workshops at one conference is not pre-mainstream. Not checked: the Xiaomi-Robotics-1 100k-hour corpus claim.

hot_topics.topic: World models as learned simulators for embodied decision making
hot_topics.why_now: Video diffusion got fast enough to run action-conditioned rollouts in real time (arXiv July 2026 reports 30-50 FPS distilled models, and one system claiming 17x speedup over diffusion baselines), so a generated video model can substitute for a hand-coded physics simulator when collecting experience. The bottleneck moved to long-horizon consistency and to measuring whether the imagined world obeys physics.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: CVPR 2025 'WorldModelBench: The First Workshop on Benchmarking World Foundation Models'; NeurIPS 2025 'Embodied World Models for Decision Making' and 'LAW 2025: Bridging Language, Agent, and World Models for Reasoning and Planning'; RSS 2026 workshop 'Robot World Models'; ICML 2026 'RLxF: RL from World Feedback'. arXiv cs.CV world-model query returned 40 papers inside a 20-day window in July 2026, naming new benchmarks Apple-PI, KineBench and VSI-Super-Wild.
hot_topics.one_line: Instead of hand-coding a physics simulator, you train a video model to predict what the camera would see next given an action, then let an agent practice inside that predicted world.

hot_topics.topic: Data-centric robot learning: demonstration quality over demonstration quantity
hot_topics.why_now: Open teleoperation data pools crossed the size where more hours stopped buying more generalization, so attention shifted to which demonstrations actually help, how to audit a mixed corpus, and how to run community data engines with quality gates rather than raw collection targets.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: RSS 2026 accepted workshops include 'Data-Centric Robotics: What Data Do Robots Really Need?' and 'It's the demos: A Deep Look at the Role of Demonstration Quality in Imitation-Based Robot Manipulation', both new for 2026. Corroborating arXiv cs.RO, 2026-07-23: 'AXIS: A Growable Community-Driven Data Engine for Scalable Robot Manipulation' and 'Scale Up Strategically: Learning Compositional Generalization via Bias-Aware Evaluation'.
hot_topics.one_line: Robot policies are trained by copying human demonstrations, and the field just recognized that a handful of sloppy demonstrations can damage a policy more than a thousand clean ones help it.
hot_topics.critic_note: Decisively overstated. Venue titles are accurate (RSS 2026 #12 'Data-Centric Robotics: What Data Do Robots Really Need?' and #4 "It's the demos", both confirmed verbatim), but the research question is five years old, not new. arXiv 2108.03298 'What Matters in Learning from Offline Human Demonstrations for Robot Manipulation' (2021-08-06) is precisely the which-demonstrations-help question. It is also thoroughly mainstream now: 2502.08623 'Robot Data Curation with Mutual Information Estimators' (2025-02-12, DeepMind and Stanford) has 509 votes and 143113 views, the highest engagement of any paper I surfaced in this audit. Surveys exist: 2508.17449 'Robotic Manipulation via Imitation Learning: Taxonomy, Evolution, Benchmark, and Challenges' (2025-08-24), 2511.03565 (2025-11-05), 2604.27621 'Robot Learning from Human Videos: A Survey' (2026-04-30). And 2603.09056 (2026-03-10) already uses the exact phrase 'data-centric robot learning' in its title. The claim that 'the field just recognized' this is the weakest sentence in the set.

hot_topics.topic: Scaling training environments for agentic RL
hot_topics.why_now: Verifiable-reward RL now works on LLMs, so the scarce resource became executable environments with automatically checkable outcomes rather than model capacity. Containerized task harnesses and auto-generated environments made it practical to train an agent inside the same harness it will be deployed in.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: NeurIPS 2025 'Workshop on Scaling Environments for Agents' (first edition) and NeurIPS 2025 'Workshop on Multi-Turn Interactions in Large Language Models' (fetched from neurips.cc/virtual/2025/events/workshop); ICML 2026 'Decision-Making from Offline Datasets to Online Adaptation'. arXiv cs.CL 2026-07-23 'OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment' and 2026-07-24 'Teaching LLMs to Self-Evolve: Cultivating Core Meta-Skills with Reinforcement Learning'.
hot_topics.one_line: The hard part of training an AI agent is no longer the model, it is building thousands of realistic sandboxes where a task can be automatically graded pass or fail.

hot_topics.topic: Agent failure diagnostics: reproducible triggers and execution-trace debugging
hot_topics.why_now: Agents reached production in 2025-2026 and fail in ways an aggregate benchmark score hides, for example a single tool-call misfire eight steps into a trajectory. That created demand for trace-level forensics, reproducible failure triggers, verified fixes, and uncertainty estimates over whole trajectories rather than single answers.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ICML 2026 accepted workshop list (icml.cc/virtual/2026/events/workshop) includes 'Failure Modes in Agentic AI: Reproducible Triggers, Trace Diagnostics, and Verified Fixes' (first edition), 'Statistical Frameworks for Uncertainty in Agentic Systems' (first edition), and 'The Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond'. arXiv cs.CL 2026-07-24 'Ground Truth First: A Longitudinal Evaluation Instrument for Agent Memory'.
hot_topics.one_line: When a multi-step AI agent fails, a single pass-fail score tells you nothing, so researchers are building tools that replay the agent's trace, isolate the exact step that broke, and prove the fix holds.
hot_topics.critic_note: Venue evidence verified verbatim on icml.cc: 'Failure Modes in Agentic AI: Reproducible Triggers, Trace Diagnostics, and Verified Fixes' (#13) and 'The Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild' (#34). Fails the survey rule outright: arXiv 2606.04990 'From Agent Traces to Trust: A Survey of Evidence Tracing and Execution Provenance in LLM Agents' (2026-06-03) is a direct survey of trace-level forensics, and 2605.14892 (2026-05-14, 50 votes) surveys failure attribution in multi-agent systems. A fault taxonomy already exists, 2603.06847 'Characterizing Faults in Agentic AI: A Taxonomy of Types, Symptoms, and Root Causes' (2026-03-06), as does a benchmark, 2604.22708 'Seeing the Whole Elephant: A Benchmark for Failure Attribution' (2026-04-24), and shipped tooling, 2607.18754 'AgentDebugX: An Open-Source Toolkit for Failure Observability, Attribution, and Recovery' (2026-07-21). When the survey, the taxonomy, the benchmark, and the open-source toolkit all exist before the workshop convenes, the topic is consolidating, not forming.

hot_topics.topic: Computer-use and GUI agents
hot_topics.why_now: Screenshot-grounded vision-language models became accurate enough to click reliably, and reproducible OS-level sandboxes turned desktop and mobile control into a scoreable task. The frontier moved off raw success rate onto inference cost, memory across long sessions, error recovery, and prompt injection arriving through on-screen content.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: arXiv abs:'GUI agents' returned a dense 2026-05-28 to 2026-07-20 stream naming benchmarks OSWorld-Verified, AndroidWorld, MacArena, LabOSBench, Workflow-GYM, LivingScreen, Memory-World and GUI-RobustEval, with stated acceptances at CVPR 2026, ECCV 2026, ICML 2026 and ACM MM 2026. Related venue: ICML 2026 workshop 'SCALE: Scalable Learning and Optimization for Efficient Multimodal AI Agents'.
hot_topics.one_line: An agent that drives a real computer by looking at the screen and clicking, now judged less on whether it can click and more on whether it stays cheap, remembers a long session, and ignores instructions planted in a web page.

hot_topics.topic: Meta-evaluation: auditing the benchmarks themselves
hot_topics.why_now: Contamination, saturated leaderboards, and LLM-as-judge feedback loops made headline scores untrustworthy, and 2026 program committees began policing evidence directly: ACL published a statement on desk-rejecting papers with hallucinated references, and EMNLP 2026 announced both an AI-reviewing experiment and a paper integrity policy.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ACL 2026 (San Diego, July 2-7) accepted workshop list includes 'Second Workshop on Evaluating Evaluations (EvalEval): Examining Best Practices for Utilizing and Developing Generative Model Evaluations' (fetched from 2026.aclweb.org/program/workshops). NeurIPS 2025 'Evaluating the Evolving LLM Lifecycle: Benchmarks, Emergent Abilities, and Scaling'. ICML 2026 'Combining Theory and Benchmarks: Towards A Virtuous Cycle to Understand and Guarantee Foundation Model Performance'.
hot_topics.one_line: Before trusting a model's benchmark score, check the benchmark itself: this line of work measures whether the test is leaky, already saturated, or skewed by the model doing the grading.

hot_topics.topic: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models
hot_topics.why_now: Streaming speech-in speech-out models made simultaneous listening and speaking technically possible, so the research problem became conversational timing: barge-in, backchannels, overlap handling, and how to score naturalness at all. Scarcity of genuine two-channel conversation data is the current wall.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ICASSP 2026 HumDial Challenge with an explicit Full-Duplex Interaction track (challenge overview on arXiv 2026-01-09, track paper 2026-04-23). About 30 arXiv papers between 2025-10 and 2026-07, including 'TurnNat: Automatic Evaluation of Turn-Taking Naturalness' (2026-07-01) and 'A Survey of Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Systems' (2026-06-17). Flagging honestly: the survey is a maturity signal, so this is past the earliest forming stage. Interspeech 2026 special-session page did not load, so no Interspeech-specific claim.
hot_topics.one_line: A voice assistant that listens and talks at the same time, handling interruptions and 'mm-hm' the way a person does, instead of waiting silently until you stop.

hot_topics.topic: Voice-clone attribution and the failure of speaker anonymization
hot_topics.why_now: Zero-shot voice cloning became a consumer feature, so binary spoof detection stopped being sufficient. The live questions are which cloning system produced a given clip, and whether anonymization pipelines survive an attacker who combines audio with video or metadata. Recent work argues there is an information-theoretic floor below which attribution is simply impossible.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: arXiv eess.AS July 2026 cluster: 'A Geometry-Limited Identification Floor and Voice-Clone Attribution' (2026-07-17), 'Multimodal Speaker Verification as a Threat to Speaker Anonymization' (2026-07-22), 'From Read Speech to Spoken Digits: A Task-Specific Evaluation of Speech Privacy' (2026-07-23), 'How Meta-Learning Shapes LoRA Adapter Geometry in Speech Deepfake Detection' (2026-07-24). Caveat: the standing challenge series (ASVspoof, VoicePrivacy, both Interspeech satellites) is recalled from prior knowledge and was not fetched this session, so treat that specific anchor as medium confidence.
hot_topics.one_line: Detecting that a voice is fake is no longer the hard part; the hard parts are naming which tool cloned it and accepting that voice anonymization can be undone by an attacker holding a second data source.

hot_topics.topic: Long-horizon controllable video generation
hot_topics.why_now: Clip-level video quality is good enough that the frontier is minutes rather than seconds: holding identity, geometry and narrative stable over long durations, and generating interactively so a user can steer mid-stream. Streaming architectures with explicit memory are displacing pure clip-level diffusion.
hot_topics.venue_evidence: ICML 2026 workshop 'From Frames to Stories (F2S): Toward Reliable, Controllable and Trustworthy Long-Horizon Video Generation' (first edition, from icml.cc/virtual/2026/events/workshop); NeurIPS 2025 'What Makes a Good Video: Next Practices in Video Generation and Evaluation'; CVPR 2025 'Visual Generative Modeling: What's After Diffusion?' and '2nd GenAI Media Generation Challenge Workshop'. arXiv July 2026 exemplars: M4World (stable minute-long streaming) and LingBot-World 2.0 (unbounded interaction horizon).
hot_topics.one_line: Moving video generation from a pretty five-second clip to a coherent several-minute scene that stays consistent and that you can steer while it plays.
hot_topics.critic_note: Decisively overstated. The topic name is close to the union of two surveys published a year earlier: arXiv 2507.07202 'A Survey on Long-Video Storytelling Generation: Architectures, Consistency, and Cinematic Quality' (2025-07-09) and 2507.16869 'Controllable Video Generation: A Survey' (2025-07-22, 84 votes). A third synthesis, 2604.06339 'Evolution of Video Generative Foundations' (2026-04-07), follows. The ICML 2026 F2S workshop title is confirmed verbatim (#10) and the venue evidence is sound, but the maturity label is not.
